Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup of the Hoyle state into three $\alpha$ particles based on measurements taken using a specialized detector called a Time Projection Chamber. The research found that almost medium-free measurements of the Hoyle state direct decay into three $\alpha$ particles show a cross-section of $0.699 \pm 0.045 \times 10^{-11}$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$ keV$^{-1}$ at 1300 MeV/c. The Hoyle state lifetime was also discovered to be 4.3$^{+0.3}_{-0.2}$ MeV/c. The Hoyle state direct-decay component is the primary feature that explains the strengths and weaknesses of the Hoyle state optical model across the 1800-1300 MeV/c energy range.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation time scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. The critical role of these scales is demonstrated in sensitivities of instability thresholds and their variations with different materials, as well as in the existence of multiple solution branches under the same boundary conditions. The length scale also affects the vulnerability of cracks to oscillatory instability, with shorter lengths scaling to nonlinear elasticity leading to more unstable behavior. The introduction of an artificial length scale in numerical models leads to incorrect predictions, with small artificial lengths suggesting an increased tendency for oscillatory instability. The fracture branch is found to be resistant to oscillations, while the other branch is dynamically unstable for a given set of initial conditions. The fracture branch is also resistant to a variety of different types of instability, while the other branch is dynamically unstable in each case. The most stable fracture branch is found to be resistant to a variety of different types of instability, and the most unstable branch is found to be resistant to oscillatory instability. The fracture branch is dynamically unstable under certain conditions and the most stable fracture branch is found to be resistant to a variety of different types of instability. The most unstable branch is found to be resistant to oscillatory instability.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and energy harvesting. The capacity of these channels with feedback is described in terms of the directed information between auxiliary variables and the channel outputs. Additionally, we propose two distinct methods for determining this capacity: a method involving the development of an infinite-horizon average-reward dynamic programming system and a method utilizing auxiliary directed graphs called Q-graphs. These methods are applied to various illustrative examples, with a particular example examining a channel with look-ahead access, for which we establish a closed-form lower bound on the capacity. Furthermore, our methods are shown to accurately calculate the capacity of well-studied channels, including unifilar channels such as the trapdoor, Ising and input-constrained erasure channels. Finally, we analyze a channel with a state transition pattern described by a regular tree, for which we establish a novel duality relationship between the channel capacity and the capacity of a related channel with a distinct state transition structure.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a non-centrosymmetric crystal structure is characterized by unusual spin-symmetric order parameters that evade Anderson's monogamy rule. Utilizing a diagrammatic approach for treating interactions in metals, we demonstrate that attractive Rashba Hubbard interactions yield a chemically stable Rashba superconducting state at the mean-field level with an energy gap proportional to the Rashba coupling constant and confined to a particular Fermi surface at the crossing point of two Fermi circles. Additionally, we establish that this spin-symmetric superconducting state exhibits topological properties, as described by a Chern number based on a particular band structure definition. Relevant experimental observations on Rashba superconductors are discussed.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to verify factual information and locate supporting evidence within tabular scientific data. The comprehensive dataset comprised 981 manually crafted tables and an automatically generated collection of 1980 tables, encompassing over 180,000 statements and more than 16 million annotated evidence references. This task comprised two primary sub-tasks. Sub-task A required participants to verify whether a statement was substantiated, contradicted, or remained inconclusive relative to a given table. Meanwhile, sub-task B involved pinpointing the specific table cells that served as evidence to support the given statement. Ultimately, a total of 69 teams entered the competition, with 19 and 12 submissions successful in sub-tasks A and B, respectively. We are about to present our results and findings from this competition.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, there's a brief examination of the transient flow scenario.

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating pollutants in flue gas emissions. A numerical model of a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) was used to simulate and analyze the removal of sulfur dioxide SO2 through gas-phase oxidation. Various UV radiation models were considered, each involving a grid convergence study to determine the optimal number of discrete light sources for maximum performance. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of residence time and reactor size on SO2 removal. Ultimately, under optimized conditions, the results show that an ozone-UV light system can be a suitable solution for sustainable air pollution control applications.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a major hurdle in the development process. To speed up simulations and increase efficiency, a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC is developed, utilizing multiple CPU cores to execute various tasks simultaneously. This virtual platform is applied to a specific neuromorphic computing system and its performance is benchmarked with standard benchmark suites, demonstrating improved simulation speeds with multi-core processors compared to traditional serial approaches.

Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into
clear, logical arguments that can be applied to other reasoning systems.

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's capacity to eliminate unproductive alignments, it was later integrated with early abandoning. A new variant of PrunedDTW, known as EAPrunedDTW, was designed with early abandoning incorporated, and it outperforms PrunedDTW in searched neighbor points. EAPrunedDTW was specifically applied in a similarity search framework, resulting in improved implementation versions, with one using multi-threading for parallel computations of pre-scaled signals. Experimental findings confirm that EAPrunedDTW enhances the efficiency of PrunedDTW in neighbor queries.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve this aspect by introducing Testing Tutor, a platform that offers various testing pedagogies and a customizable feedback engine. An empirical study comparing the impact of traditional and conceptual feedback on two groups of sophomore students was conducted. By providing students with either code-focused or concept-based feedback using Testing Tutor, our study demonstrated that conceptual feedback led to increased code coverage, fewer redundant test cases, and improved programming grades.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using symbolic machine learning to construct explicit models covering specific scenarios, thereby enabling the production of more detailed, feature-level explanations for neural networks through an innovative two-stage process. Firstly, concepts are identified based on associated features, then symbolic models incorporating these concepts are created to showcase the intricate features driving network decisions. This new approach is evaluated on existing datasets and contrasted with alternative methods in an exhaustive comparison. According to the results, it outperforms other comparison methods in accuracy and precision and substantially reduces the number of artificial examples required. This novel framework shows great promise in uncovering the underlying features driving neural network decisions, particularly in uncovering the underlying features driving neural network decisions.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of its lower limit and the influence of dataset size and over-smoothing countermeasures. Furthermore, solutions to overcome over-smoothing are evaluated and the findings suggest that multi-layer graph neural networks can indeed be effective despite over-smoothing.

Dark matter particle research focuses on a hypothesized particle pair creation accompanied by a Z boson decay into electrons or muons. This study utilizes a large dataset of proton-proton collisions, equivalent to 35.9 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the CMS experiment. It analyzes particles produced in events involving a Z boson and one or two opposite-sign dileptons, with invisible particles presumed to be dark matter particles. By comparing observed counts to theoretical predictions based on the standard model, researchers set limits on the cross-sectional values of two theoretical scenarios involving a mediator boson. One scenario has a broad width and involves both electron and muon visible particles, while the other scenario has a narrow width and involves only one electron visible particles. When combining the results of this study and previous studies, researchers have reached their strongest limits to date on the two scenarios, with the first scenario having a limit of 43.2 pb and the second scenario having a limit of 45.4 pb.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with the same support size or as a subset of the group of homeomorphisms of its compactified space. A space has the CSHP if these two definitions yield the same topological space, which is the main topic of the paper's methods to prove that product spaces of specific spaces with CSHP possess CSHP.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or even what values some important statistics have. By using information about the matrix of average relationships among these time series, we can make accurate inferences about common random patterns under minimal conditions. Even when individual observations are rare, this matrix can be estimated reliably. Through simulations and real-world examples, we show that this method can give more accurate inferences than others under a specific set of conditions. A testable condition reveals that these inferences become highly accurate when a key assumption holds, leading to optimal performance. Our method is particularly useful for understanding financial and currency exchange data, which often exhibit extreme fluctuations.

JWST has identified multiple early galaxy candidates in the strongly lensed cluster, ACT-CL J0102$-$4915, through observations by the Optical/Infrared Camera. These observations were carried out in the second month of JWST operations, utilizing the instrument's full field of view and near-infrared channels. Analysis of the observations placed an estimated upper limit on the near-infrared sensitivity threshold at 2.6 $\mu$Jy, enabling the detection of extremely dim objects that are magnified by a factor of at least eight due to strong-strong gravitational lensing in the area. The data show multiple bright sources, each consisting of multiple components, within the area covered by the Multiple Arcs Wide-Field Infrared Survey (MAWIFS). These sources include nine early galaxy candidates, each exhibiting multiple features. The detection of multiple features suggests that the galaxies are quite extended, given the correction for the effects of the strong gravitational lensing. The estimated redshifts for the galaxies range from 3 to 6, as determined through observations in the wavelength range from 1.3 to 5.2 $\mu$m. The data indicate the presence of a population of stars observed through near-infrared polarimetry in one of the early galaxy candidates. The distribution of the uncovered stellar populations is observed across the area covered by the MAWIFS. The data suggest that the strong gravitational lensing in the area places significant constraints on the parameters of the incompressible intra

Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced service quality by the ISPs. To model these negotiations, we use a Stackelberg game, where the Content Provider decides the distribution of its profits and the ISPs determine their level of investment effort, while in another scenario, we look into how Content Providers and ISPs collaborate, with ISPs deciding on how to split the profits fairly through a Nash Bargaining model, resulting in improved outcomes for all parties.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as an inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship capturing key aspects of the algebraic data preserved throughout the process. This adjoint relationship categorically renders the algebraic data equivalent, implying the data can be recovered precisely from the underlying Hilbert space representation of the C*-algebra.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory hold great promise in the context of upcoming cosmological observations, also having connections to supergravity. Exponential and polynomial models of this type are compared against recent data from the field (notably the 2018 Planck dataset combined with findings from BICEP2 and the Keck array), yielding specific model predictions along with optimal values for associated parameters. The assessment relies on integrated software tools: ModeChord, CosmoMC, and PolyChord, operating in tandem.

In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold with a boundary that approaches infinity, its foliations measured at infinity directly relate to the horizontal measured foliations derived from the uniformization maps associated with its components that extend towards infinity. For a given hyperbolic surface that a pair of measured foliations, denoted by $\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}$, completely fill, our analysis reveals that when sufficiently small, multiplying both $\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}$ by a factor of $t>0$ results in unique representations as the foliations measured at infinity for a corresponding quasi-Fuchsian three-dimensional manifold. This new manifold is essentially an extended version of the given surface that approaches an infinite real number. Our finding is similar to another known theorem which asserts that a nearly Fuchsian three-dimensional manifold is uniquely defined based on certain characteristics of its boundary that approach infinity. Our results are also validated by numerical data.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to concentration than those from the mean-variance model.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, a new dataset has been introduced, capturing the effects of both types of distortions.  A leading approach in literature, AstLaS, is evaluated on this new dataset and compared against four alternative methods.  The new dataset is based on recordings from subjects with a specific heart condition as well as noisy recordings obtained using different devices and backgrounds.  The findings suggest that existing models can struggle with sounds that have both types of distortions, highlighting a need for improved methods.  The research suggests that developing heart condition detection algorithms based on high-quality recordings may not be enough, and instead, algorithms need to be capable of handling the variations in conditions as well as noises that are commonly encountered in the field.

In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about a part of this calculation and provided an alternative calculation for the same quantity. However, our calculation and the one raised by Roberts and Ginges have different limitations and apply to different conditions. While Roberts and Ginges's calculation is appropriate for realistic nuclear environments, our original condition was meant to enhance the relativistic coupled-cluster results and was not meant to be a final answer. We agree with Roberts and Ginges that our original result needed further refinement and welcome their result as a significant improvement.

A twist is utilized as a localized element in the study of topological K-theory. 
Within the framework of equivariant analysis, twists are categorized into four distinct forms, which can be visualized geometrically. 
This paper examines all possible forms of twists for a torus with actions imposed by 2D space groups, and equivalently, all finite subgroups in the torus's mapping class group. 
The study employs calculations involving Borel's equivariant cohomology and the Leray-Serre spectral sequence to achieve its goals. 
As an additional outcome, the equivariant cohomology up to the third degree is found in all instances, and connections are also drawn with twists related to Freed-Moore K-theory.

Pomona College's Mathematics & Statistics Department has been dedicated to
establishing an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students to
engage in mathematical study. In response to low diversity among majors, the
department initially attempted to address this through targeted programs aimed
at enhancing students' mathematical abilities. Conversely, recent efforts have
shifted to an anti-deficit strategy, which prioritizes modifying the
department's internal culture to foster a more cohesive community. Our
initiatives to boost collaboration, atmosphere, and overall department
climate are detailed below.

We examine the boundedness of the fractional series operator $T_{\gamma}$, with its given function form $(T_{\gamma}b)(j)$, in the context of $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $\ell^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, a counter-example demonstrates that the operator $T_{\gamma}$ does not yield a bounded mapping from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from the auction rules, but when participating in an uncredible auction, typically don't prioritize maximizing revenue. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences.

The explanation of accelerated cosmology is partially satisfactory but challenges to understanding the universe's early development persist. Our research focuses on the potential of a new symmetric teleparallel theory of gravity, denoted as $f(Q)$, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ helps to address theoretical issues in gravity's fundamental representation. To tackle the universe's initial phase, we establish a model based on a specific type of spacetime with both rotation and anisotropy and then derive equations governing the model's motion. By analyzing energy density, the relationship between energy and pressure, and spatial geometry characteristics, we find that this theoretical framework supports spatial geometry evolution due to both rotational and anisotropic influences. However, we also find that certain constraints can lead to spatial geometry alignment and ultimately isotropy, despite initial anisotropy. Our study provides insight into the universe's initial phase from a novel gravity framework and addresses key theoretical issues in this framework.

We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg subvarieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart based on the maximal element of the Weyl group corresponding to GL(n,ℂ). This allows us to express local defining ideals as an square-free monomial ideal combined with quadratic binomials, which we prove to be independent of the choice of Hessenberg function. By analyzing the generators of this local ideal, we demonstrate that it forms a geometric vertex decomposition, thereby obtaining a Gröbner basis for the ideal associated with the variety using a combination of standard Gröbner basis methods and the Frobenius splitting technique. Consequently, this analysis yields explicit decompositions of local fields and vector bundle modules, as well as certain projective Hessenberg varieties of type A.

Neural Painters, utilizing a GAN-based approach, generate brushstrokes that are assembled into paintings. Despite GANs' superiority in AI-generated art, their training can be exceptionally challenging. To address these difficulties and accelerate Neural Painter training, we employed Transfer Learning, achieving a notable time reduction from days to just hours without compromising visual quality. Our findings are presented in this study.

We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the introduction of heavy flavorful vector bosons at an energy scale of $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$. If these vector bosons are substantially heavier, around $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ or above, a problem arises, as we then encounter difficulty in resolving the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly consistently with the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mixing constraints. However, the proposed framework is compatible with the given data within the one-sigma confidence threshold for each anomaly, with the parameter space to be examined by experiments such as NA62 and KOTO and through direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over research papers. For each question, multiple answers are provided, accompanied by supporting justifications that cite relevant paper sections. This structure requires subtasks like Question-Candidate Matching, Answer-Categorization, Justification-Copy Editing, and so on to evaluate human performance. Experimental results on the full QASPER dataset demonstrate the difficulty of these subtasks for current models, including the notable underperforming of BERT. Additionally, the paper presents results from model predictions on multiple training data variants, starting with a single sentence, and observes the importance of having the full question for accurate answer predictions. Lastly, the team plans to continuously update the QASPER dataset, now available at: https://github.com/juajuste/qasper.

In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, only the explosive model exhibited instability behind the shockwave due to the interaction between particles and neutrinos. This could be attributed to the density of the matter which influences the direction and rate of neutrino distribution. Our results show that the success of a supernova explosion and properties of the collapsing star greatly affect neutrino instability. Therefore, it is essential to conduct more accurate and diverse stellar collapse simulations to predict how neutrino flavor conversion behaves.

ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies, which often relied on the entire brain, this study focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning model. By using rsfMRI data from the ADHD 200 global competition, the researchers employed leave-one-site-out cross-validation to derive an integrated outcome. Notably, the study found that using merely 15 crucial regions of interest for training yielded a 70.6% accuracy rate, surpassing the 68.6% accuracy achieved when using the entire brain. Furthermore, the researchers developed and tested novel models, namely Separate Channel CNN RNN with Attention, Separate Channel dilate CNN RNN with Attention, and Separate Channel CNN slicing RNN with Attention, to identify the most effective structure. The ASSRNN model emerged as the top performer, attaining a 70.46% accuracy rate with an average loss of 0.1716, highlighting its potential for applying deep learning models to diagnose ADHD.

In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where population growth is constant and balanced, the per capita mortality and fertility rates are equivalent, and the model's evolution operator is a nonlinear function of seven parameters. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry. As a result, an electron charge current can be directed from hot to cold or vice versa, and an accompanying heat current is also predicted. These findings can be attributed to a simple and logical physical interpretation. Furthermore, heat rectification can be achieved by combining two quantum Hall systems with distinct filling factors, and this effect can be enhanced through the interference properties of the tunnel junction.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired index variations, allowing us to efficiently implement the desired indexing structure within each data segment. We've implemented and tested our proposed DNA-storage method on a laboratory-scale DNA storage setup and demonstrated its practical applicability and efficiency under current DNA storage technology limitations.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines.

In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronization across entire systems and are prevalent in many biological and chemical processes. These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker cells, serve as a means of transmitting information at a constant speed over extended distances. This research utilizes advanced analytical tools to explore how environmental factors affecting pacemaker cells impact the speed of generated waves, specifically those caused by excitatory and inhibitory dynamics. By applying multiscale modeling, we were able to derive precise mathematical equations for wave velocity across diverse ecological settings, ranging from minimal to complex mechanisms. Our analysis reveals how sensitive wave speed is to the spatial distribution of resources, as well as how it is affected by changes in the pacemaker area, transitions between different behavioral states, and adaptations in challenging environments. Additionally, we observed a unique relationship between wave speed and the frequency of oscillations in the pacemaker, which has significant implications for its functional behavior.

A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, leading to diverse applications across theoretical and practical domains. The focus is on determining approximations within a factor $\gamma > 1$ of the Shannon entropy in probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy in mixed quantum states. The key contributions are two algorithms: a quantum one for approximating Shannon entropy that requires $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries, and another for approximating von Neumann entropy that necessitates $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries. These results hold provided the entropy is bounded away from zero by a quantity linked to $\eta > 0$, and a no-go result indicates the non-existence of polynomial query algorithms for distributions with very low entropy. The analysis considers the most general input model - the quantum purified query access model - enabling handling of both classical distributions and quantum states. The study also establishes a lower bound on query complexity at $\Omega(n^{\frac{1}{3\gamma^2}})$ for approximating Shannon and von Neumann entropies multiplicatively.

Implementing innovative Artificial Intelligence (AI), throughout an entire enterprise, necessitates thorough expertise in foundational AI technology. This expertise encompasses computing, network infrastructure, data centers, data management and security, which are essential elements for constructing reliable AI systems. Effective storage solutions, used across various applications, are particularly crucial in preserving AI model data, used for operations like model updates, file sharing and issue resolution. Maintaining separate data centers, versus relying on cloud services, also introduces distinct advantages and hurdles. Furthermore, developing high-quality AI models necessitates an understanding of computing and data processing, including parallel processing, distributed systems and data dissemination. This knowledge is further elaborated upon in the sections below.

Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, a task known as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Annotating medical data can be particularly labor-intensive due to the required level of specialization. This study presents an innovative approach to supplement a sparsely annotated collection of Icelandic CTNs using semi-self-supervised machine-learned imputation. By initially training a neural network on a small number of annotated CTNs, the model extracts clinical characteristics from un-annotated CTNs, generating around a thousand additional training examples. These newly created cases facilitate the training of a second neural network to predict diagnoses based on CTNs. When applied to data from the Icelandic healthcare system, the implemented approach demonstrated coding accuracy above chance for nearly three-quarters of diagnosed conditions, while boosting overall coding precision and recall compared to a system trained on sparse data alone.

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation required for its implementation. A significant obstacle is overcome by quantum computers, which may offer an exponential improvement in processing capabilities. This study delves into the development and execution of both unsupervised and supervised learning algorithms on a quantum device. Specifically, we demonstrate quantum versions of k-means, Gaussian mixture model fitting, binary classification, and logistic regression, all of which are successfully implemented on a superconducting quantum device. By comparing these quantum algorithms to their classical counterparts, we find them to be notably more efficient in terms of computation required, albeit with the caveat that current experimental results are impeded by noise which needs to be mitigated in future studies.

Our analysis encompasses all prime-field microlensing planets from the 2018 dataset provided by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder, revealing 24 total discoveries or recoveries, 11 of which were previously unpublished. Among these, six published studies focused on planetary systems comprising multiple planets, while another two explored planetary systems comprising two linked bodies. Conversely, 11 anomalies lacked accompanying secondary body data. This data analysis yields 18 new planetary systems, increasing the total count to 134, according to the Exoplanet Encyclopedia. Graphical illustrations accompany the data findings.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images.

Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this paper develops an innovative framework to estimate the average and statistical relationship of origin-destination demand while considering the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections. The framework also determines the probability distribution of link and path flow along with their associated costs and optimizes traffic flow while managing origin-destination demand and network flow uncertainty. A probabilistic linear complementarity algorithm and a probabilistic successive shortest path algorithm are proposed to solve the respective optimization problems. The effectiveness of the framework is demonstrated through numerical tests using real-world traffic data from Atlanta and Los Angeles.

In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in the system, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of stability, akin to that observed in nearly conservative systems. The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where the oscillations' amplitudes are eliminated under an adiabatic process.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on complete graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate uniform spanning trees in tandem. This realization enables a faster, hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both algorithms to expedite uniform spanning tree generation in complete graphs. Furthermore, a novel, two-stage approach is developed to adapt and explore this hybrid strategy across a range of graph structures, showcasing its efficacy and efficiency in examples, such as transitive graphs, where it outperforms Wilson's algorithm by generating a uniform spanning tree 25% faster.

This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia data. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our research expands on existing musical notation, combining it with audio synthesis and generated sheet-music images to create a dataset with precise alignments among audio, visual, and text-based components. This aligned MusicTM-Dataset allows for the development of joint representation learning methods among musical audio, sheet-music images, and lyrical text. By representing multiple modalities through a unified framework, our approach demonstrates impressive results in cross-modal retrieval tasks, surpassing traditional two-modal approaches significantly. To facilitate reproducibility, our code and dataset are freely accessible on GitHub and GitHub.com/mm-ait-team/MusicTM-Dataset.

One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the interface enhances user experience. This integration demonstrates how natural language and visual interfaces can be synergistically combined to simplify the exploration and understanding of complex Linked Data entities and their relationships within Ontodia and Wikidata.

We've discovered that in the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation with variable refractive index and a defocusing cubic nonlinearity, dark solitons display the same characteristics as in the pure cubic defocusing model. However, adding variable refractive index significantly changes how we assess stability in the dark solitons. Notably, only isolated imaginary axis eigenvalues are found, and energy-based stability is applicable with exponentially weighted Sobolev spaces. Moreover, adding small external influences and confinement still yields spectrally stable solitons in the minimum points. The system's solitons persist as small waves travel through it, and we take this behavior into account when investigating the overall stability of dark solitons.

This collaborative approach in visual analytics aims to facilitate seamless interaction between humans and machines, according to various established frameworks. To bridge the gap between theoretical foundations and practical implementation, we introduce an intuitive model for system-assisted guidance and a corresponding library. We present a model for system-supplied guidance based on predefined templates and derived methods. Furthermore, we create the Lotse library, allowing developers to specify guidance strategies using definition files and automatically generate functional code. The Lotse library offers an innovative approach by providing reusable guidance templates for easily creating various guidance methods. Through case studies involving VA researchers with different levels of expertise, we demonstrate the library's capability to accelerate development and enhance usability. The Lotse library is freely available for download at https://lotse.github.io.

We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Our research reveals that stellarator design can be both quasisymmetric and exhibit excellent performance even when the rotational transform is not close to zero.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, with temperatures at the bottom of the bed surpassing those at the top by up to 30°C. The temperature discrepancies are attributed to convection and conduction inconsistencies within the system, highlighting the significance of advection in gas-solid systems. The presented MRI thermometry technique offers promising possibilities for system optimization and understanding gas-solid interactions through dynamic studies.

Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to understand condensate self-assembly, interactions between a large number of different molecular species were studied and programmed to test for variability and rules. The number of different droplets formed from mixtures increased significantly as the number of different molecular species in the mixtures increased. The maximum number of different droplets in a mixture could be accurately predicted even without full knowledge of all interactions. The models' simulations confirmed these expectations and suggested the underlying rules for spatial organization through droplets could be widely applied across cellular molecular mixtures.

Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major leading sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 during two powerful solar flares. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced significantly by the solar eruptions. Moving disturbances within other sunspots, caused by the solar flares, traveled rapidly and altered the magnetic properties associated with the sunspots in question, providing valuable insights into the dynamic process governing the sunspots' development.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the study examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the research compares the computational efficiency of BDDC and AMG implementations on two distinct cardiac mechanics codes, highlighting differences in runtime scalability associated with different runtime systems (OpenMPI and Intel C++ Parallel Studio) and compiler flags.

The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing these systems based on usage patterns, the evolution of user-generated content over time, and the underlying social dynamics.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order.

This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ decay rate is given by $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, with any positive integer $l$. Through the application of the time-weighted energy method, we manage to enhance this rate to $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Under the condition that the frequencies are sufficiently low, by incorporating the principles of the Littlewood-Paley theory, we find that the solutions have properties belonging to certain Besov spaces of negative order and establish the most favorable $L^2$ decay rate.

Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through wireless connections offers a promising way to develop flexible and high-density networks that can be deployed both mobile and fixed outdoors. Mobile IAB, in particular, has the potential to enable a range of innovative applications by allowing wireless access devices to move freely. This work provides a comprehensive overview of the progress made so far in developing mobile IAB solutions by surveying existing research in academic journals and conferences. Our analysis focuses on the key problems that need to be addressed by future studies and highlights areas where further research is required.

In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of five leading global optimization algorithms as a hyperparameter configuration problem, utilizing three different methods to evaluate the sensitivity of their adjusting parameters. Our investigation leverages the NSGA-II, MESA, COBYLA, PSWCHA, and Bayesian optimization algorithms to solve a variety of benchmark functions, allowing us to compare the effectiveness of hyperparameters across different scenarios. Furthermore, we determine the optimal ranges for key parameters, such as the Mueller-Regis schedule, allowing future researchers to select from pre-calculated options to accelerate their experiments. Our analysis also highlights the advantages and limitations of each method, suggesting the appropriability of certain techniques for specific problems. Consequently, this study provides valuable guidelines for researchers in the field.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, with certain approaches showing promise in specific settings, although a critical limitation is the lack of standardized evaluation tools for comparing these models across different scenarios. To help address this issue, we present Lifelong Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge simulation environment that allows researchers to assess the capabilities of continual learning models in various learning and forgetting regimes. This extensive platform offers a range of built-in challenges, incorporating elements such as exploration induced forgetting and task shifting, offering a versatile framework for the development and evaluation of robust and adaptable reinforcement learning algorithms.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory.

This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity $H^s$ for $s<3/2$. The velocity of these waves is directly proportional to their distance from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions in Gevrey spaces, where a damping mechanism prevents long-term perturbations. This research is particularly notable given that it contrasts with previous results showing no non-trivial travelling waves in areas immediately surrounding Couette flow with regularity higher than $3/2$.

We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations including non-local gradient elements. The specific focus lies within a particular class of nonlocal problems formulated within a given domain in higher dimensions. The formulation is based on an equation where the fractional Laplacian of a variable $u$ is equal to the sum of a nonlinear term derived from $\nabla u$ and another term derived from $\nabla u^2$, all bounded within a given nonlocal framework. The specific nonlocal framework employed involves considerations on differences between variables defined on a given nonlocal foundation. The given nonlocal foundation is based on a foundation with an exponential decay, specifically with powers of $|x-y|^{-n-q\alpha}$. The given nonlocal foundation is also considered with a nonlocal element involving a kernel represented as $C\min\{|x-y|^n, 1\}$. The specific proof requirements involve the establishment of continuity and monotonicity of solutions, as well as considerations on existence and uniqueness of the given nonlocal problems. The specific class of nonlocal problems is further represented by an involved system of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations, specifically with terms involving $u^2$ and $\delta u^2$, all within a given nonlocal framework and with considerations on necessary boundary conditions.

The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system's functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. To combat the lack of real-time data, false information, and health-related myths in South Africa, we developed an unsupervised machine learning approach to analyze available news articles regarding COVID-19. By using wordpiece tokens from the BERT model, our proposed framework effectively captured the vocabulary's variations. The experiment revealed that using BERT alone yielded coefficients indicating a strong positive correlation, supporting the global efforts to mitigate the pandemic.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this theorem by probing the extent of the similarity given a sumset of a specific size, specifically when it's just above 2k-4.

In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables healthcare professionals to form more precise opinions. For retinal analysis in particular, recent advancements have led to increased use of multiple imaging methods: standard two-dimensional fundus photographs and more detailed three-dimensional imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography. Our study employed three distinct multimodal fusion strategies centered on deep learning to tackle challenges related to fundus image analysis: early combination, intermediate fusion, and hierarchical integration. Noting that early combination and intermediate fusion approaches demand uniform data formats for their information fusion methods, they were applied to single-dimensional fundus photos and paired two-dimensional photos plus OCT features. In contrast, hierarchical integration was used with various combinations of three-dimensional imaging data, which included both OCT and OCT angiography. Our findings showed that a specific hierarchical approach yielded the most accurate results for diagnosing and predicting severity of glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy compared to other methods, with an exceptional accuracy rate of 96.7% for DR diagnosis.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive potential for severe COVID-19 cases.  If accurate, this could facilitate early severe case prediction via chest X-ray images, thus enabling healthcare professionals to implement proactive treatment strategies.  However, the features allegedly linked to severe cases require thorough examination due to concerns surrounding their reliability and clinical implications.  This study aimed to identify and assess potential features associated with severe cases using 1,184 X-ray images from 308 patients who developed severe COVID-19.  Notably, six features were consistently present in patients with severe cases, which were then validated using validation sets from two independent datasets, resulting in accurate detection rates exceeding 90%.  Furthermore, the results showed that patients with severe cases exhibited more pronounced lung abnormalities, consistent with previous studies.  These findings highlight the presence of distinct radiological features distinguishing patients with severe cases from those with non-severe cases.

We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, \sigma, \mathbf{n}^2)$. Considering the case where $\Omega$ is a 2 or 3-dimensional ball, and the functions $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only depend on the radial distance $r$, we find a sequence of transmission eigenfunctions that tend to concentrate their energies around the boundary of $\Omega$ as the associated wavenumbers $k$ increase without bound. If $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ are constant, we prove the existence of transmission eigenfunctions that become localized around the boundary of $\Omega$. Our results generalize the recent studies in the mentioned literature and also illustrate the influence of medium parameters $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ on the geometric patterns of transmission eigenfunctions via numerical experiments.

To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, or require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to representing utterances semantically and clustering them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that leverages a large amount of unlabeled data in conjunction with labeled external data for representation learning. Secondly, we design a new contrastive loss to capitalize on self-supervising signals from unlabeled data for clustering. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the substantial improvement achieved by our method over existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art results with an impressive 12.3% increase in F1-score.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.
In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups.

This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0,0 and S1,0. A detailed analysis reveals that ADAE H2 can be simplified into a sixth-order hyperbolic-type equation. Additionally, a subset of the direct linear scheme's subalgebra is generated by the actions of three bistochastic B-spline collocation matrix operators. The researchers also investigate the impact of nonlocal boundary conditions on the Cauchy matrix scheme, demonstrating that it remains in the subalgebra. A new set of L2-orthogonal polynomials is defined in reference to the underlying ADAE H2.

This paper delves into the domain of Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) to counter a major issue that arises during model testing, namely the abundance of false positive predictions. In order to tackle this problem, we first need to understand the source of these errors by extracting low-level features from images. To improve upon existing approaches, we propose to utilize Super Resolution (SR) techniques to increase the resolution of extracted features, thereby gaining insight into the low-level features. A novel design for the model's architecture is suggested, one that integrates object detection and relationship prediction as a single entity to minimize errors and streamline training procedures. Additionally, we introduce the concept of relationship-based proposal ranking to eliminate irrelevant proposals by filtering out relationships that do not match as predicted relationships. A significant decrease in false positives and state-of-the-art performance on three datasets (VG-150K, VG-SAT and FP-VG) are achieved with our proposed method.

A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the target state's trace norm and hyponorm, as well as the overlap with the probe, with the lowest bound achieved through optimal quantum measurement methods. Furthermore, our results reveal that the QCC plays a crucial role in the optimal quantum correlation cost (EQCC), with EQCC reduced by QCC in optimal quantum correlation cost (OCC). This relationship means that EQCC and OCC share the same asymptotic behavior as OC, indicating that OCC's asymptotic behavior is insensitive to quantum correlation, whereas OC's is sensitive.

Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Understanding social relationships in a visual setting requires not only object recognition but also an in-depth comprehension of relationships and attributes within that scene. An end-to-end neural network capable of generating social relationship graphs from images is presented in this study. It leverages an image feature extraction module, based on ResNet, and incorporates a relationship graph generation module, featuring a relationship-aware graph generator along with a supervised fuller context model. Additionally, it utilizes the finder module to locate individuals and groups within an image according to a predefined reference system. Extensive testing on the Social Relationship Graphs (SRG) dataset demonstrates that our proposed network outperforms existing techniques, while also showcasing versatile applications, such as generating social relationship graphs from images and identifying individuals and groups based on their social context.

Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but comes with prohibitively high computational costs. We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph for message passing, thereby reducing computational complexity compared to prior approaches. This allows us to design a self-attention module and a new Transformer-based backbone that outperforms state-of-the-art models in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters. The code and models will be publicly available.
