Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders used in the MCM circuit and demonstrates a strong correlation with the energy consumption and latency. Our enhanced model accommodates various integer bases and can be solved through an improved ILP formula. Additionally, we introduce two new optimization techniques: a dynamic coefficient reordering method and a coefficient rounding strategy, both reducing the required memory to store MCM coefficients. Our revised ILP model and associated tools significantly outperform the existing approaches, yielding faster computation times and better solutions. Specifically, our model and accompanying source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/yzech/MCM.git.

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously being separate entities, advancements have revealed that quantum circuits share parallels with artificial neural networks, paving the way for widespread adoption. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way. It also explores the challenges inherent in quantum deep learning research, touching upon promising prospects such as enhanced simulation capabilities and light-touch solution options.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to be fundamental in 
high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, where significant progress has been 
made over the past decade in advancing the field. This progress could soon lead 
to upgraded existing facilities, enhancements to facilities still under 
construction (such as PIP-II), well-established proposals, or newly emerging 
ideas like the FCC-ee and future proton intensity upgrade at Fermilab, among 
others. Innovations in RF technology not only contribute to HEP but also extend 
beyond to fields such as nuclear physics, basic energy sciences, and other areas, 
as evidenced by European XFEL, LCLS-II, and other free-electron laser (FEL) 
projects. This report aims to summarize RF technology R&D findings over the 
past decade and foresee potential advancements to come.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves, aligning with kinetic theory. This agrees with numerical simulations in Einstein-Hubbard model.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments.

Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processing with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to enable Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) at a secure computing offloading level, such as cloud computing. The VSP safeguard against internal threats like malicious hardware and external threats like phishing and data exploitation. To achieve this, our innovative approach incorporates a custom-made FHE library and a novel processor architecture, featuring a five-stage pipeline, designed specifically to execute VSP code over FHE at a high instruction-level. Moreover, to increase the processor's efficiency, we introduced two groundbreaking techniques: Circuit Overhead Reduction by Tokenizing Comparisons (CORTC) and Tokenized Circuit Evaluation with Shared Tokens (TECST). Experimental results demonstrate that the VSP processing speed matches that of a non-secure processor, with negligible latency and increased memory requirements. For instance, VSP executes 43.69 microoperations per millisecond with approximately 18KB memory needs. Consequently, the adoption of VSP processing becomes both feasible and efficient, opening the door to widespread use in practical applications and scenarios.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, well-known sparse graph classes such as forest, matchoid, and cactus graphs, and it also yields better approximation ratios for classes where Baker's method achieves a QPTAS.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments demonstrate the significance of linear projection matrices in self-attention for accurate parsing. Consequently, the unsupervised models were transformed into few-shot parsing models, FPOA and FPIO, to achieve impressive results on minimal datasets.

High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into a novel application, specifically employing hyperspectral images for cityscape object segmentation using an unsupervised learning approach that circumvents the need for manual object classification. This method capitalizes on the rich spectral data inherent in HSI images, which facilitates efficient object segmentation within complex urban environments. By analyzing the inherent properties of HSI images and developing a corresponding segmentation framework, we demonstrate how these images can improve low-quality labels, ultimately leading to higher accuracy in object segmentation. Our results demonstrate that this technique produces competitive results and outperforms manually refined labels in certain scenarios. Moreover, the refined labels derived from HSI images contribute significantly to the enhancement of object segmentation. This research validates the significant potential of HSI images in advanced visual applications, showcasing improved results compared to the current standards. The resulting hyperspectral segmentation labels have the capacity to enhance a range of vision tasks, including object recognition, semantic segmentation, and medical diagnostics.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, presenting an intriguing anomaly. Possible explanations for this anomaly include the star's interaction with a planetary body or the presence of internal waves promoting mixing within the star. Despite these theories, more comprehensive research is needed to thoroughly understand the internal rotation dynamics of this star as well as others like it.

In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This study aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. The proposed base RAM model has limited storage and processing capabilities, allowing for exponential time to perform basic arithmetic operations like subtraction and multiplication. This work presents a revised RAM model that resolves these issues by introducing novel, efficient algorithms for these operations, along with division, using only addition. The model also yields a comprehensive characterization of LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin by revealing that linear-time computability on ordered domains relies on the existence of constant-time multiplication. Additionally, the study explores the relationship between the new RAM model and existing probabilistic computability classes, such as #P and PP, through which it demonstrates that CONST-DELAY-lin corresponds to the class #P.

To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets.

This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a subring of $n \times n$ matrices, resulting in LCD codes that are also group codes due to being ideals in a group ring. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes, with additional constraints enabling the development of reversible group LCD codes. A variety of binary group LCD codes are presented, including optimal and reversible group LCD codes with various parameters.

We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, the proposed method allows for the creation of arrays with sizes $L \times \ell$ where $L$ ranges from 2 to 10 and $\ell$ can be any natural number. These findings are presented in a comprehensive table. The findings of this research have practical implications for wireless communication systems employing omnidirectional precoding techniques.

Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. The constraints on non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons align with the standard model predictions in on-shell and off-shell regions. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 MeV, while the simulated expected range is between -8 and 12 MeV. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain comparable with the simulated expected constraints when considering the standard model coupling structure.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. By integrating various techniques to extract changes from the images, it significantly outperformed current state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised change detection across diverse datasets.

Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$ of squares and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a subset of natural numbers such that when you combine these two sets with addition, the result encompasses all natural numbers greater than or equal to some finite number $N_0$. Now, the $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ denotes the count of all possible pairs of $s$ from $\mathcal{S}$ and $w$ from $\mathcal{W}$ whose sum is equal to $n$. Previous studies, led by Harper and Savage, showed for a specific $N$ that the total count of such pairs for all natural numbers $n$ less than or equal to $N$ is dominated by an expression of $N$ raised by a power of $\frac{1}{2}$. This paper changes the scope from pairs to systems consisting of one $s$ from $\mathcal{S}$ and one $w$ from $\mathcal{W}$ and finds a lower bound for the total count $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ of such systems for all natural numbers $n$ in a given interval. Moreover, we determine the exact order of this lower bound in comparison to the total count $\mathcal{W}+\mathcal{S}$ of natural numbers in set $\mathcal{W}$ combined with the set $\

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that allows particles to transfer from one atom to another. This interaction can result in either constructive or destructive outcomes, depending on the relative positions and properties of the involved atoms. In silicon, atomically precise placement of dopant atoms is crucial for optimizing the material's properties by quantifying the wave-like behavior of electrons at the atomic level. By utilizing a quantum modeling approach, researchers have developed a framework to systematically evaluate the different effects contributing to tunneling behavior, including the alignment of electron spins and valley states unique to silicon. Valley interference effects are identified as a key factor driving the varying levels of spin exchange between silicon atoms located above a copper surface. Specifically, a notable variation in spin exchange is observed when placing dopant atoms in different silicon valleys, indicating a significant valley interference effect. Consequently, researchers suggest that valley interference could be harnessed to develop highly accurate atomic-scale tools for inspecting silicon materials used in advanced quantum technology applications.

Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world scenarios, hence their importance is being increasingly acknowledged by the community. As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovation in both techniques and their practical applications. In the context of this study, we introduce a novel framework, known as LibOPT, for efficiently implementing and prototyping nature-inspired optimization algorithms. By integrating 15 established techniques and 112 benchmark functions, as well as supporting 11 novel hypercomplex-based approaches, our framework surpasses others in its domain, thus marking it as a groundbreaking innovation in optimization software development. Utilizing LibOPT under the C paradigm proves to be remarkably user-friendly and adaptable, as evidenced by the inclusion of clear source-code examples demonstrating the practical usage of benchmark functions.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures.

In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are described by non-abelian space symmetries represented by a four-momentum group. Our approach recognizes that for multi-particle states, the total system momentum is the only well-defined property. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition of individual particle momenta, which become ambiguous. Our results indicate that previous Fock space constructions were flawed due to incorrect assumptions and lack success. We demonstrate that momentum exchange underlies a relativistic covariance principle in the braiding of quantum numbers, solving a persistent challenge in the field.

We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties of wide bandgap semiconductors. We utilize this technique to
investigate charge transport in scCVD diamond by exciting its charge carriers
with a femtosecond laser. Due to its two-photon nature, the technique confines
charge carrier generation in 3-D around the laser focal point. This localized
charge injection enables us to study the semiconductor bulk with high 3-D
resolution. We mapped the diamond's bulk electrical field at varying depths by
taking advantage of charge spatial confinement. The results were then compared
to X-ray diffraction topography. The approach allows for unique insights into
spatial charge transport variations in transparent wide bandgap materials.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their non-multitask counterparts. Our findings indicate that the first place win was accomplished by a BERT-based model capable of distinguishing between non-misogynistic, general misogynistic, and severe misogynistic content, also demonstrating the superiority of multitask learning over baseline models in this novel application.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust when faced with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that controllers developed from a probabilistic Gaussian Process model are robust in the sense defined. This theory offers conditions under which this robustness is certain and provides a method to determine the degree of robustness. We test the theory on a simulated inverted pendulum and reveal that a controller's robustness is directly related to the uncertainty in the model. Based on these findings, we propose an approach that enables the efficient search for controllers robust against uncertainty by reducing the scope of policy search by minimizing predicted variances. This predictive variance constraint also offers a way to quantify the trade-off between expected rewards and structural robustness. We demonstrate that this approach yields a superior controller in both performance and robustness on the tested scenario and also on a set of simulated robotic tasks.

Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework enables connections between caching schemes and numerous combinatorial objects, offering versatility in scheme design. We show that various distributed computation methods can be rationalized through a straightforward'stacking' process, allowing existing caching schemes to be applied directly to obtain desirable computation results. We also develop new caching schemes with improved efficiency using our framework, along with general bounds on delivery latency and storage efficiency.

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike previous approaches to dealing with partiality.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a major challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we provide a solid foundation for quantum operations, derived from solving evolution equations, and build upon this base with control techniques and efficient state sampling methods to develop practical nonlinear gates, especially a nonlinear Hadamard gate. Furthermore, our work in BEC interferometry and quantum computing redefines the paradigm by incorporating principles from nonlinear quantum mechanics, effectively applying it to interferometry and information processing.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, leveraging a specific set of initial assumptions. Notably, it is assumed that the mappings are non-degenerate and share a particular characteristic with a given meromorphic mapping, which is itself derived from a combination of constants and transcendental functions. Secondly, the paper seeks to prove a unicity theorem for the case of non-tranendental entire meromorphic mappings that encounter a specific type of obstruction – a hyperplane that is invariant across an entire manifold –  and are further constrained by a particular set of conditions involving their orders of vanishing. To achieve these objectives, the authors draw heavily upon an extensive body of work, including recent findings and develop novel applications of a unicity technique that incorporates an infinite series of differential forms, which was first outlined in an earlier paper by the first author and colleagues.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons significantly contribute to the photon spectrum. In Cu$+$Cu collisions, photons show a clear increase above a binary-scaled $p$$+$$p$ fit, and their transverse momentum spectra follow a similar trend as Au$+$Au collisions, involving a similar number of participants. We have determined the inverse slopes of the photon excess spectra at $285\pm53$(stat)$\pm57$(syst) MeV/$c$ and $333\pm72$(stat)$\pm45$(syst) MeV/$c$ for minimum bias and most central events, respectively. Moreover, we found that the photon rapidity density in Cu$+$Cu demonstrates a similar power-law behavior versus charged particle multiplicity observed in Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new technique for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a scaled limit and invariance under vertex blow-up.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL's default anti-aliasing capability lead to unintended artifacts and increased rendering times when utilizing this technology. In order to overcome these challenges, a simplified yet effective anti-aliasing method was developed by modifying an OpenGL pipeline using a frame buffer object. This innovative approach employs two primary vectors to replicate line ends, allowing for accurate anti-aliasing while preventing misalignment and reducing artifacts by leveraging the fragmant depth buffer. Moreover, this anti-aliasing method can be easily integrated into existing mapping applications without requiring substantial modifications to code.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values.  In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance.  Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity.  It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results.  Numerical experiments confirm that the new interpolation method outperforms the original W-S scheme in approximation accuracy while maintaining equivalent order convergence rates.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications on the puzzles of excess positrons and the widespread TeV gamma-ray excess. Lastly, we outline the prospective research avenues based on the anticipation of discovering more pulsar halos and carrying out deeper investigations into the brightest sources.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of monitoring weather engage both human observation and technological means, but are often too limited or expensive to provide the quick coverage needed for real-time traffic management.
Image recognition technology has the potential to significantly enhance weather monitoring accuracy and speed.
We introduce a recently developed high-resolution weather image dataset encompassing eight categories and 32 subclasses.
The dataset spans from 27000 to 30000 images, offering a more precise segmentation of weather conditions.
A novel data augmentation technique is introduced to mitigate class imbalance.
A comprehensive assessment of machine learning models is conducted, including the implementation of transfer learning on pre-trained CNNs, weighted loss functions, and sample selection synthesis.

Our specific contributions are as follows:

A new large-scale weather image dataset with precise classifications is introduced.
A groundbreaking data augmentation approach is established to counteract class imbalance.
A comprehensive evaluation of convolutional neural networks is conducted, incorporating weighted loss functions and sample selection synthesis.

The proposed dataset and techniques are shown to significantly improve weather detection accuracy across multiple categories and subclasses, reaching an impressive 93.96% overall accuracy with a 97.91% recognition rate for subclass classification.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our analysis of UK data since 2005, contrasting with a relatively stable trend among economics professors, as shown in the analysis of Journal of Environmental Economics data spanning 1990 to 2008. Interestingly, climate change interest among scientists appears to be stable, as revealed by examining publications in the journal Climatic Change between 1800 and 2008. We observe a notable decrease in climate change interest among economists following the 2007-2008 global financial crisis, as shown in our analysis of Journal of Environmental Economics data from 1990 to 2009. We propose several explanations for this phenomenon, including the argument that many economists primarily view climate change through the lens of a market failure, and therefore, the sharp economic downturn may have reduced the perceived need for further discussion on the topic. Our study also explores other potential drivers of the observed fluctuations in economists' interest in climate change, emphasizing the importance of ongoing institutional and scientific developments in maintaining a sustained area of interest.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time physical robot control requirements. In this research, we propose an innovative online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update and refine a dynamic model in real-time. By integrating the updated model into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) structure, our approach enables successful deployment on multi-fingered soft robotic grippers. Our results demonstrate a high success rate in grasping diverse objects, even those initially unknown to the controller, as compared to other model-extraction methods. Additionally, our approach has been validated through a series of experimental trials, as showcased in a publicly available video.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost cost function cost(s,x). Various optimization techniques have been developed to address this issue, with some methods, such as gradient descent, struggling to yield significant progress at the edge of local optima. Natural Gradient Descent, having a superior convergence rate, still falls short in several aspects - it doesn't guarantee global optimality, lacks a comprehensive theoretical foundation, and is computationally expensive due to its large memory requirement. This paper introduces new methods to enhance NGD's practicality. Our research shows that a particular parameter regime of NGD can be reduced to gradient descent, explaining its failure to surpass human capabilities. To overcome this limitation, we have developed an adaptive algorithm called Generalized NGD, providing a theoretical framework for its effectiveness and presenting empirical evidence of its superior performance in machine learning applications.

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies should make up a significant portion of these distant galaxy populations. This study uses a highly detailed analysis of data collected from multiple observations of a particularly old and distant galaxy called J2102+6015. High-resolution imaging of J2102+6015's energy emissions, which were captured through a highly precise technique called VLBI at a wavelength of 8.4 GHz, revealed two distinct energy-producing regions. This imaging revealed two distinct energy-producing regions aligned east to west that displayed flat or reversed spectra. Importantly, the separation between these regions has changed very little over a 13 year period. Consequently, the speed at which the energy regions move is thought to be less than about 0.04 arc-seconds per year. In addition, our detailed analysis indicates that J2102+6015 is very likely a younger, dense and symmetric structure rather than the core of a highly energetic active galaxy as had been suggested by earlier studies.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing the forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then used various techniques to compile a new set of features and conducted
experiments to determine the most effective ones. Ultimately, we constructed and evaluated
a high-performing LSTM network to classify Twitter posts as either positive, negative, or
neutral.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled as the superposition of individual memory pulses and investigated the resulting stochastic background using a specific source model. They calculated the spectrum and amplitudes of the SGWMB and explored how they're impacted by parameters such as inclination angle and frequency range. Notably, the SGWMB's spectrum and characteristics overpower those of more commonly studied gravitational wave sources, including binary black hole mergers and pulsar chirps, within a certain frequency range. Researchers concluded that the SGWMB is likely to be detectable by next-generation gravitational wave observatories and that its detection will significantly advance our understanding of high-energy physics and the binary black hole merger process.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; this framework predicts the universe underwent a phase transition around the time of the universe's birth that may create ripples in space time that scientists could detect. Developing a realistic model based on how this supersymmetry is broken, researchers found this model predicts a type of particle decay that could explain a specific, intense particle shower observed coming from the PeV-scale. The same supersymmetry mechanism also predicts ripples in space time that match current predictions for gravitational waves produced by the early universe. Additionally, the universe's initial conditions could lead to the creation of tiny, dense objects called black holes that may have existed in the early universe and could soon be detected through a new detector called the Einstein Telescope. The discovery of these cosmic phenomena could significantly advance the understanding of the universe's earliest moments.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design a context-specific communication language, an alternating maximization algorithm optimizes utility values between communication nodes. This language enhances the vocabulary for message transmission by splitting complex data into simpler components and allows for generalization to unforeseen scenarios. A neural network model is used to reconstruct causal states based on the relevant data attributes at the transmitter, which are then evaluated by a receiver that implements a symbolic logical formula execution using AI components. Specifically, this implementation leverages the Generative Flow Networks tool for improved semantic reliability. This communication system has been designed to evaluate a new set of metrics, such as semantic information and distortion, using rigorous category theory algebraic properties, expanding beyond traditional notions of uncertainty as defined by Shannon. Simulation results demonstrate the system's capability to transmit data more efficiently with enhanced reliability compared to conventional wireless systems and existing solutions without causal reasoning capabilities.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics but disregards syntactic rules governing word contexts within a sentence. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes; however, they often overlook the coherence of predicted words, leading to subpar results in continuous word prediction tasks. In response to these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid word prediction model, combining the effectiveness of Naive Bayes and latent semantic analysis to address the word prediction challenge. The model's performance was validated using the Wikipedia Redirects dataset and the resulting predictions, demonstrating substantial improvements over existing models.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network and demonstrates the potential through Candidate Rank Embedding in re-ranking. Experimental results demonstrate a considerable enhancement over the baseline on metrics such as Recall, MRR, and Click-Through-Rate in an online setting, and we further observed improvements when applied to STAMP and NARM models on two public real-world datasets for the task of next-click prediction.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 257 fractures spanning 4.76 meters in length.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. A more efficient method is required to tackle these challenges, especially since traditional approaches rely on high-energy interventions. A near-real-time algorithm is developed to address these issues, leveraging a registration technique based on point clouds, which proves more effective than existing methods. Experimental outcomes of this algorithm are presented in simulations and real-world tests conducted with drones. Results indicate that this algorithm outperforms others in collision avoidance, requiring less energy and processing time.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of negative eigenvalues, the eigenvalue bounds, the characteristic polynomial, and the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which are subsequently substantiated with numerical examples.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving an delayed consumption optimization problem and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints, both driven by fractional Brownian motion.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance network performance in this challenging environment, this research employs stochastic geometry to develop an analytical model comprising RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicles. Assuming relays are deployed at specific intervals along roads and utilize a single frequency, we analyze the coverage area of RSUs, vehicle relays, and vehicles, before examining network performance metrics such as blocking probability, effective signal probability, and outage probability for both macro and micro relays. Furthermore, this research introduces a novel method for determining the distance between vehicles and RSUs, which is initially derived as a binary distribution and is subsequently expressed as a continuous random variable. Simulation results validate the accuracy of the analytical model, showing that the proposed method outperforms existing solutions.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually generated labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors' behavior provides more accurate labels compared to crowdworkers who lack the same level of contextual understanding and agreement as editors.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering clear group-theoretic criteria for classifying classical T-duals and providing explicit, continuous-trace algebra computations for the resulting non-trivial Dixmier-Douady classes. Ultimately, we demonstrate that any solvmanifold can be represented as a $C^*$-algebra bundle of noncommutative tori, which we explicitly compute, while the monodromy of the original torus bundle is translated into a Morita equivalence among fiber algebras.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging guidance from human experts.  However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical due to the time and resources required.  A new technique has been developed to overcome this limitation by leveraging the behavior of experienced agents without requiring direct oversight from humans.  The imitation learning method in question incorporates elements from its traditional counterparts, including Leveraged Imitation Learning (LIL) and Generalized Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL), yet adapts these components to learn from the actions of existing agents without needing explicit labeling or costly human supervision.  The proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art imitations by achieving notable improvements when applied to classic cart-pole and robotic arm scenarios.  The results suggest that the potential benefits from transferring knowledge across diverse agents, also known as the knowledge transfer effect (KTE), can be substantial, with our approach yielding a 300% increase in cart-pole rewards and up to a 120% improvement in robotic arm tasks.  The novel framework supports a range of emergent scenarios, including agent-centric, state-based, and action-based learning, thereby providing more flexibility and generalizability to the existing ACL literature.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which enhance average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate improved performance via the proposed metric function, with superior error-correction performance and significantly reduced computations. In some instances, our optimal 128-bit codes outperform existing best 256-bit PAC codes, showcasing the potential benefits of our metric function and decoding approach.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use an efficient module that generates object SDF data from the first frame and performs optimization-based tracking. Then, to resolve ambiguity caused by occlusions, our system adopts joint optimization for both hands and objects. In our training process, our system only uses simulated, highly variable synthetic data for ease of generalization, making our system highly effective even on real-world, highly occluded hand-object interaction datasets. Our results show impressive tracking and reconstruction performance on such challenging sequences, outperforming current state-of-the-art 3D hand tracking and object tracking methods.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star, it's possible for these particles to interact through a hypothetical particle and release neutrinos in the process, which could lead to intense neutrino bursts and potentially reveal clues about dark matter. Initially, it's assumed that reactions within the star's core follow standard nuclear equations, although it's recognized that interactions involving particles other than neutrons and protons may occur. In the specific case of a hypothetical particle called a pseudoscalar, it's possible for it to interact with other particles in the star, which could lead to enhanced neutrino production. New calculations for this type of interaction predict a significant increase in neutrino emissions, which could reach tens of percent and potentially reach levels of thousands percent above previously predicted rates. As a result, even relatively small amounts of dark matter particles in a star could still result in enhanced neutrino emissions, which must be considered in future studies.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 40 million galaxies, translating to a density of 6.8 per square arcminute. A low-level systematic bias was found in galaxy shape measurement, contributing no more than 0.6 microarcsecond^2 uncertainty. Applying our newly developed ShapePipe measurement pipeline demonstrated excellent agreement with the ngmix standard, yielding a measured cosmological power spectrum accuracy of better than two percent and a present signal-to-noise ratio of 47 for a specific cosmological model. In the upcoming stages of UNIONS, the survey will expand to a further 4500 square degrees, offering enhanced sensitivity with a signal-to-noise ratio of 100.

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that a certain number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and another number $b$ in the interval $(0,1)$ differs from the rotation sequence for no integer $m$, then, as $N$ approaches infinity, the parity of the sizes of sets consisting of numbers of the form $\{q\alpha\}$ within the interval $[0,b)$ that correspond to $q$ values up to $N$ displays evenly distributed occurrences.

The text also discusses how it answers a query put forth by Veech, thereby providing a revised mod $n$ form of a prior result (as stated in Theorem 3.1). A characterization, based on specific values, of scenarios where evenly distributed occurrences result (especially when $b$ equals the rotation sequence for some natural number $m$ and $\alpha$ is an irrational number) is also proposed (as stated in Theorem 2.1).
