We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally determined parameters are employed to determine the critical temperatures associated with BKT transitions as well as long-range order. Finite-size scaling of the spin stiffness based on our in-plane theory shows a perfect match between theoretical and experimental critical temperatures, clearly indicating that the complex magnetic phase diagram of [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 is determined by field-induced XY anisotropy and concomitant BKT physics.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate various DM composition ratios to observable differences in phases, ratios, and spectra, ultimately enabling future DM direct detection experiments and forthcoming CMB experiments such as CMB-S4 to test the model by distinguishing between various DM composition ratios.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically controlled quantum circuits, utilizing a novel concept introduced in arXiv:1803.02724. The key innovation involves deriving stronger upper limits on the number of stabilizing states associated with each magic state, using a procedure independent of specific quantum algorithms. The upper limits derived in this study outperform previous estimates and remain versatile, applicable to any magic state defined by a group homomorphism.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by evaluating the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, namely non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the plausibility of these scenarios as real universe descriptions 
by calculating the fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, and analyzing two parts 
of the quintessence field effect: the complex and real parts. We assume the real part 
behaves as a slow-roll field.
We understand that scenarios with a fractional energy density ($\Omega_{D} > 1$) do not 
accurately depict real universes. Furthermore, we introduce an interacting coupling 
parameter, $P$, and learn that although the value of $\Omega_{D}$ may be within 
expected ranges for non-interacting scenarios, it may exceed this range in interacting 
scenarios.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized the SDSS Vault's medium-resolution spectra to train machine learning models. These models demonstrated excellent performance, with the stellar parameter calculation accuracy within 0.05% and the radial velocity accuracy at 0.08 km/s for our sample of 2643 stars. Furthermore, the research team developed a new method for identifying binary and multiple star systems using low-resolution spectroscopic data. This new method effectively distinguished systems with radial velocity variations from those with static lines and avoided misidentifying single stars as binary systems. Ultimately, the analysis revealed 463 binary and 34 multiple star systems. To establish radial velocity variations, the research team applied a simplified least-squares method for 264

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two commercial FPGA boards. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance with respect to throughput, energy consumption, and latency.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process information at extremely fast rates and also exhibit long-lasting memory due to a low leakage current. Additionally, simulations have shown that it is feasible to achieve both volatile and permanent storage capabilities within the molecules by controlling their electronic charge.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be achieved through the use of mathematical operations known as Borel transforms and contour deformations. By utilizing this causal representation, common loop-induced divergences are eliminated, allowing for a more straightforward numerical evaluation of multi-loop Feynman integrals. Furthermore, the causal representation by itself provides a divergent, yet physically valid result that is dependent on the specific choice of contour, offering a new perspective on the problem.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing for a direct computation of the spectral measure in a particular model known as the two-phase model.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a $q$-deformed optomechanical system, comprising two deformed cavities interacting with bulk and surface defects. The work showcases that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows, along with amplifying non-traditional light effects within the system. Furthermore, the study establishes a connection between the $q$-deformation and hybridization within the system's mechanical oscillator, highlighting that $q$-deformation can increase the efficacy of light coupling by up to twice the standard value.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored a R-parity violating scenario, resulting in negative R-parity scissors modes appearing with reduced collectivity and lower energy compared to their positive counterparts. As a result, these negative R-parity modes are expected to be less intense in electric dipole transitions, potentially leading to a simpler 0+0 scenario in the Euclidean limit and reduced sensitivity to side-feeding branches during the transition.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique material properties.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical dynamics, resulting in "anomalous" diffusion that accounts for distributions characterized by long, power-law tails. One such physical system - laser-cooled atomic ensembles - offers an optimal platform to study such phenomena, primarily due to its distinctive friction force. This interplay between laser cooling and anomalous dynamics is likely to reveal profound and predictive insights into both equilibrium and non-equilibrium statistical physics. In experiments involving cold-atom systems, scientists can manipulate and adjust various system parameters to observe changes in the system's behavior, and this has been achieved by analyzing non-normalized states associated with rare events, utilizing tools derived from infinite ergodic theory, resulting in new findings.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are examined using Granger causality and O-information to quantify both pairwise and high-order statistical relationships. The Granger causality results indicate peaks in significant events, while the corresponding network structure exhibits stability, with most influential nodes being cryptocurrencies. Analysis reveals divergent patterns in European and Asian time zones, with US dollars serving as a primary driver of network dynamics. Additionally, a high correlation exists between the number of pairwise and triadic relationships within subnetworks and their corresponding network complexities. The research further reveals that non-linear interactions, captured through the information flow, predominate over pairwise Granger causality in pricing cryptocurrency assets, implying the significance of higher-order effects in this context. The study suggests evaluating high-order statistical relationships in financial markets more thoroughly.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely dilute conditions. The application of quantum chemistry allows researchers to investigate the chemistry of cloud-forming species with varying levels of approximation. In this study, we compare the performance of the statistical thermodynamic model and the path integral hyperplane-approximation in reproducing the results of high-level quantum chemical calculations of sulphuric acid and water clusters. The results show that for small clusters containing four or more molecules, the statistical thermodynamic model is sufficient, but the use of higher-level methods, such as CCSD(T), is required to accurately account for certain cluster configurations. The benefits of utilizing more comprehensive theoretical frameworks are most evident in the context of zeta-point energy calculations, which influence the stability of certain clusters and need to be addressed through the use of higher-order methods like CCSD(T).

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a totally bounded subset of their codomain, resulting in a compact space of images, now taking on the role of perceptions. These results draw parallels with established compactification techniques for metric spaces, fundamental work by Borsuk, Nagy, and others having laid the groundwork.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals that this thermal analogy does not hold; while an uneven gravitational force induces specific energy flows, a comparable uneven temperature has little to no effect in systems that exchange energy with their surroundings weakly. Additionally, the similarity between an external electric charge and the system's internal energy potential is also invalid under these circumstances.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. We demonstrate that popular model architectures, including residual networks, batch normalization, and ensemble models, incorporate inductive biases that favor simpler solutions, effectively acting as regulators of geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a highly accurate automated essay grading model.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particles.  Together, the signals for these boson combinations indicate a cross-section of boson production that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual boson combinations have been detected at 3.4 (expected to be 3.2), 3.3 (expected to be 3.1), and 2.3 (expected to be 2.1) standard deviations above background noise for three particular combinations of bosons, respectively.  Together, the detected occurrences of these boson combinations are at least as significant as 4.3 (expected to be 4.7) standard deviations above background noise for individual boson production signals.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated corpus lacks modern language characteristics, obtained through social media and various other platforms. As a result, attempts to directly apply advanced NLP models have yielded subpar results. This paper addresses the necessity for a new, extensively annotated Hebrew corpus. After conducting a comprehensive analysis of current available resources, a new, extensively annotated corpus was created through.ud.hebrew annotations. Utilizing Porter-stemmed words for compatibility with existing resources, the new corpus comprises 10,000 sentences from contemporary sources and 9,000 sentences from various Israel-based news articles. A basic UD Hebrew model was developed, achieving 94.5 F-score for parsing on the BNC-Hebrew corpus and 79.5 F-score on the Hebrew NLP TACHION dataset. Additionally, the new Hebrew model achieved impressive results on several English out-of-domain datasets, outperforming the standard UD English model by a significant 1.25 F-score margin.

It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the dimension $d$ is less than or equal to $\frac{32e^2 (2K)^{2p}\log n}{\varepsilon^2}$, and for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, the inequality $ \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} - \varepsilon \leq \|y_i - y_j\|_{\ell_p^d}^p \leq \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} + \varepsilon$ holds. Additionally, an algorithm which computes $\{y_i\}_{i=1}^n$ after taking $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n$ as input exists and relies on techniques from empirical method and combinatorial theory along with $L_p(\mu)$ factorization theory. Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking solution, using a versatile family of neural networks that can seamlessly incorporate information from multiple sources. This innovation enables different teams to contribute to a common model, and enables the model to accurately predict a wide range of outcomes by leveraging the knowledge gained from many tasks. The teams can collaborate by sharing their datasets, enhancing the model's overall capabilities and demonstrating substantial improvements in outcome predictions. This cooperative modeling approach shows exceptional promise in solving complex problems that require extensive data and intricate physics predictions, such as turbulence.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet the influence of pretraining corpora on this capability is relatively unexplored. To better understand this, we conducted an experiment comparing the performance of models pre-trained on books and Wikipedia articles. Our results show that changes in the pretraining corpus affect the model's capacity for in-context learning, influencing its applicability in real-world scenarios. Additionally, we discovered that data-specific errors can persist even after training on high-gradient tasks, highlighting the need for in-context learning model selection to be tailored to the domain of target tasks to optimize its efficacy. Our findings shed new light on the relationship between pretraining corpora and in-context learning, urging further research into model customization based on the domain of available data to unlock its full potential.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations that combined artificial viscosity and artificial heat, varying six key factors including magnetic field strength, cooling rate, thermal conductivity, and initial bubble radius. The results indicate that nebulae ultimately collapse into kiloparsec-scale, filamentary clouds due to conduction-driven instability, before producing new star clusters through a combination of cloud fragmentation and run-away star formation. The creation of these star clusters occurs at a slower rate when the initial bubble radius is larger and when magnetic fields suppress cooling, thus hindering the growth of new cluster stars. The duration needed for these star clusters to form is extended when the initial bubble radius is larger by a factor of 100, when magnetic fields weaken by a factor of 10, and when the initial cloud radius increases by a factor of 10. These findings provide new insight into the origins of galaxy cluster field stars.

a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive

$K^0_{\scriptscriptstyle S}\to \pi^0\pi^0$ and $K^0_{\scriptstyle S}\to

\to \pi^0\pi^0$, $\pi^0 K^0$, and $\eta K^0$. The discussion concludes

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of newly calculated high-energy amplitudes in superstring theory is consistent with those from recently discovered fermion interactions in string theory.

To meet the growing demands of future networks, companies are developing new technologies such as IoT, VR, and augmented reality. This requires supply-side network resources like spectrum, energy, and equipment to be efficiently allocated and managed. Existing network management systems have weaknesses dealing with power consumption, spectrum allocation, and equipment deployment. This research explores new methods for online network management by developing self-healing, self-organizing, and sustainable core network models under dynamic and changing conditions. We present a multi-agent model for real-time core network management across multiple domains, including wireless communication, transport, and packet switching, to optimize energy efficiency, spectrum efficiency, and service quality. Our digital twin-based simulation results show that the proposed agents can effectively manage core networks and achieve better outcomes compared to traditional methods.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental units of speech in the training data, extracting transcripts via a unsupervised end-to-end model, and employing neural networks with a parallel structure for GMM-based speech synthesis. The proposed approach significantly improves the quality of synthesized speech with a reduced mean opinion score of 3.11, surpassing previously reported scores on the ZeroSpeech dataset with a 0.40 margin.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot protocols and develop close upper and lower bounds for multi-copy versions.
Conversely, we introduced a different approach focused on the overall success probability of protocols constrained by the metric.
This new framework enabled the derivation of tighter bounds for the probability of achieving specific outcomes in multi-copy experiments and revealed more stringent limitations on the probability of success in such experiments.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also means that less-strong magnetic fields are required to produce the high-velocity jets. For very high mass accumulation rates, the high-velocity jets appear initially, but quickly weaken and then disappear completely, which makes it impossible for these low-velocity outflows to form early in the protostar formation process, especially in magnetic clouds that are very weak. The findings suggest that it is impossible for both high-velocity jets and low-velocity outflows to exist at the same time, which means that it is impossible for both to appear soon after the start of the star-forming process.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error, which ultimately enables comprehensive compensation and performance restoration. It is acknowledged that within a safety zone, certain thresholds exist beyond which compensation is impractical due to the inherent limitations of the system. The proposed framework thereby establishes a fundamental balance between system performance and operational sustainability. The methodology is illustrated through its application to a filtered van der Pol oscillator example.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect a small object orbiting the Earth, specifically considering its shape and size to determine how they impact its resonance zones. For the purpose of analysis, we divided the problem into three distinct sections, focusing separately on the effects of the Sun, Moon, and other major planets. To gain insight into the Sun's impact, we developed mathematical models that account for the phenomenon of resonance, using approximations such as the Ehlers model and the Routh model. To investigate the Moon's effects, we identified the existing parameters influencing lunar gravity and analyzed the resulting commensurabilities, ultimately plotting the resonance zones graphically. Finally, we explored the potential impacts of other planets, plotting the resonance zones for the most significant cases and providing numerical data for additional planets, including their mass and orbital distances.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to determine the 3D pose and shape of an object. Our first achievement is developing PACE3D* and PACE2D*, which are novel optimisation algorithms ensuring accurate results for both 3D and 2D keypoint data, through the use of precise mathematical formulations. Additionally, we have developed versions of these algorithms robust to outlier data, labelled PACE3D# and PACE2D#, with a framework called ROBIN for identifying and pruning these errors by utilising a graph theory method to identify compatible data sets. Our research also includes thorough testing with various simulated datasets and a real PASCAL dataset, which highlights the effectiveness of PACE3D# and PACE2D# over existing solutions.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using straightforward formulas.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria, comparing the new treatment to a control, by clinically relevant standards. For subgroups with pre-defined similarities, we find the minimum required trial sizes simultaneously. Our approach resembles frequentist methods when there's no sharing of data. Notably, by allowing data borrowing, we find smaller trial sizes needed than traditional methods that don't share information. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach using two actual trials. Further simulations demonstrate our approach maintains accuracy in detecting positive results without increasing false positives.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, limiting the speed of motion control systems despite their potential. To overcome this, this study introduces a cutting-edge control approach known as LPV sequential loop closing, which combines real-time feedback from a high-precision sensor and takes into account the effects of motion, tension, and cable sag for optimal results. To test this approach, a motion control system was built and tested, with experimental results showing significant improvements in closed-loop behavior and precision, outperforming conventional control methods by a notable margin.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict keypoints and correspondence across varying views and objects, while its geometric representation is also transferable to classification tasks.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, if one fixed inner automorphism $\varphi$ generates an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes, we then determine all automorphisms $\varphi$ that result in an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. Furthermore, we establish the criteria under which an automorphism $\varphi$ generates a finite number of twisted conjugacy classes. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups and their nilpotent subgroups, identifying those whose nilpotent quotients are isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z} \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_p^{\mathbb{N}}$ or \mathbb{Z} \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_p^{\mathbb{N}} \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_2 for some prime number p.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found at future colliders, 
we consider a different possibility where there isn't any. In this case, 
our main goal would be to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities. A crucial step to reach this goal is to determine the instability threshold of the Higgs potential. Achieving this requires substantial statistics, approximately one million four-lepton events, which can be gathered at various colliders such as the LHC, its upgrade, and three new collider projects under study (a future hadron collider with 27-31 TeV, a collider with 100-1000 TeV, and three leptonic colliders). We assess the sensitivity of these colliders to establish the SM instability threshold, comparing their capabilities based on different criteria. As a result, we find the following order of sensitivity: the future hadron collider, the collider with high energy, the LHC with its upgrade, the charged colliders, and the leptonic colliders.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties, largely due to the considerable time and resources needed to obtain reliable annotations for training deep learning models.  This paper introduces an unsupervised Cyclic Segmentation GAN, combining CycleGAN and SEGAN for SEM images, to overcome this problem.  By leveraging CycleGAN to generate synthetic labeled images from the unseen modality, and incorporating these cycles into a SEGAN framework for SEM image segmentation, the CSGAN approach minimizes discards synthetic data.  This novel method utilizes two networks:  a generator network transforming an unseen modality image into a labeled segmentation;  and a discriminator network discriminating real from synthetic segmentation labels to guide the generator network towards producing more accurate synthetic labels.  The CSGAN approach facilitates the reliable use of synthetic labels in segmentation tasks, and in our experiments with various histopathology images, the CSGAN method consistently produced synthetic labels with comparable quality to manually annotated labels.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron equipped with an RBF
kernel layer to accurately forecast actions. In our experiments, Feature Mapping RNN
achieved superior performance on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction datasets
compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum fluxes needed to supplement flare spectra observed from space telescopes. This research specifically analyzes a well-documented flare on AD Leo as observed through IUE satellite data, and employs an improved model for its photosphere to accurately self-consistently calculate energy fluxes and electron fluxes, which are then used to determine key modeling parameters including the photospheric pressure and temperature, size of the photosphere, and energy distribution of electrons. These parameters are further utilized to explain the self-absorption features observed in the UV lines, and predict fluxes at specific wavelengths in the far-UV range up to 1670 Angstroms. By modeling the time-variable flux distributions during this flare, peak energy distributions are estimated and compared with earlier models, which revealed lower energy levels in the present models, and indicate that energy release on AD Leo occurred over a time period ranging from 38 to 92 seconds

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic collection of significant p-core p'-partitions that establish a substantial lower limit on their maximum size.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: scalable, rotatable and movable and then develop a framework for ensuring the robustness of neural network-based point cloud models against deceptive attacks. The key benefit of our approach is that it doesn't need an extensive and tiresome transformation matrix, and it is flexible enough to be expanded to cover various types of transformations with minimal modifications. The results of experiments carried out on diverse 3D datasets show the advantages of TPC over current techniques in terms of performance and the speed at which it processes data. For instance, on the ModelNet42 dataset, TPC delivered exceptional enhancement in accuracy following an attack, surpassing the score of 93%, which is significantly higher than the 71% achieved by PSM. Furthermore, TPC processed samples significantly faster, with a remarkable acceleration of 20 times over PSM.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease interference probabilities. We introduce a clear channel assessment process, known as medium sensing, for CSMA, also defining metrics to gauge its effectiveness. In our analysis of CSMA, radar units transmit data after confirming an empty transmission path. We examine CSMA's medium sensing success rate, interference probabilities, and system efficiency under different system parameters. Unlike standard communication networks, the optimal strategy in some scenarios may involve the highest feasible attempt rates for maximizing throughput. Extensive simulations are conducted to validate our analytical findings and compare the efficiency of slotted ALOHA and CSMA. In our analysis, CSMA consistently outperforms ALOHA across all practical use cases.

Recent experiments employing various methods for generating entangled two-photon states A and B have sparked considerable interest in studying HOM interference patterns when photons from states A and B are directed at a beam splitter. Our study focuses on analyzing HOM interference patterns resulting from entangled two-photon states absorbed by a series combination of a beam splitter and a nonlinear optical device capable of inducing entanglement via two-photon absorption. Specifically, we examine two scenarios: one involving horizontal polarizations and the other involving vertical polarizations. By utilizing a beam splitter model with input fields exhibiting random phase, we derived formulae for interference patterns resulting from both cases. Our findings demonstrate that for the horizontal polarization scenario, a typical HOM interference pattern is observed, whereas the vertical polarization scenario yields an altered interference pattern due to the two-photon absorption effect. Notably, we identified key relationships between the absorbed spectral considerations and interference pattern maxima and minima. Our research presents an original interpretation of HOM interference patterns in the context of entangled two-photon states through two-photon absorption effects.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at a shallow angle relative to the listener's location.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily focused on perfect correlations derived from quantum systems. This has naturally led to questions about whether perfect inequalities are necessary for establishing "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to expectations, research answers this query in the affirmative by developing a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in chiral systems with an imbalance in sublattices fall into this category. Following a general description of constructing flat bands through MOs, various examples are examined with numerical proof, including the sawtooth lattice in one dimension and the hyper-Pyrochlore lattice across any number of dimensions, extending the principles seen in two-dimensional Kagome and three-dimensional Pyrochlore lattices.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. The results show that the boron-hydrogen bonds impede the formation of a dense electron gas necessary for superconductivity in this material. Additionally, our findings suggest the boron-hydrogen bonds also hinder the operation of phonon-mediated pairing in this system, contradicting initial assumptions about its superconducting potential. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that the hydrogen boride monolayer is not expected to exhibit superconductivity below its estimated critical temperature of 5.1 K.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here coincidentally relate to the numbers a(n) where n is a natural number, describing the count of ways to divide n into a sum of distinct positive integers. Specifically, we derive expressions for the nth term of two related sequences, r_n being the sum of a(k)...a(k-2l) for l = 0 to (k-1).

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain level of independence in its structure, we prove that the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, and have a certain level of complexity, exhibit rigidity as well.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this capacity, prompting us to propose an advanced method centered around formal verification, leveraging model checking in particular. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we carefully recreate the driving system's dynamics, define and formalize key safety criteria, and scope the analysis within the guidelines specified by ISO 26262. Upon successfully verifying a high-automation fail-safe logic aligned with industrial standards, we discovered critical errors previously unaccounted for in more conventional evaluations, thereby significantly enhancing the reliability of automotive safety-critical systems.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. Current methods for detecting communities are primarily grounded in static network analysis, assuming a static system. However, this is an unrealistic assumption for numerous real-world systems, which often exhibit dynamic evolution. In this research, we present a novel approach based on linear algebra that enables the identification of communities in dynamic systems by representing relationships over time. Our model utilizes influence measures and is capable of handling large amounts of data, even when system dynamics are unknown. Our approach can efficiently reduce a massive state transition matrix, facilitating the identification of stable clusters and enabling accurate clustering on various datasets. Compared to existing methods, our approach produces superior results on numerous empirical test cases. Additionally, we offer detailed algorithms and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through numerical simulations involving synthetic and real-world data.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for the perturbation theory model and compare these to simulations, focusing on HI intensity mapping at intermediate redshift (z=0.5) with a galaxy-like bias model. We analyze the predictions of linear perturbation theory, including matter nonlinearity effects, bias effects, and the impact of shot noise. We also investigate the predictions of higher-order perturbation theory models, examining their differences from the linear model, and making predictions for the related bias parameters. Through simulations, we quantify the effects of shot noise and line dispersion on these predictions. We consider two foreground removal techniques: linear Taylor expansion and Legendre polynomial Taylor expansion, and find that they remove matter nonlinearity effects but not bias effects. We use simulations to quantify the accuracy of these predictions, including the impact of residual shot noise and line dispersion. We find that at $k \lesssim 2$ rad/m, linear perturbation theory predictions closely match simulated values from HI intensity mapping experiments. We make perturbation theory predictions for the Power Spectrum Amplitude bias parameter $A_\mathcal{P}$ and the Line Width Distribution bias parameter $W_\sigma$. We find that these parameters influence the one-dimensional Power Spectrum Amplitude bias effect and the two-dimensional QPM bias effect in a linear relationship. We use simulations to constrain these parameters, and find their values to be $A_\mathcal{P} = 0.15 \pm 0

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we show that if a condition such as $T(e^x)=e^{1+x}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, then the domain of $T$ must be isomorphic to the real numbers.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with context-aware document models by taking into account the users' perspectives on these items. Additionally, our model offers the advantage of online personalization where the system can adjust the user and item representation profiles upon detecting new user interactions without requiring updates to the model's parameters. Our proposed algorithm was tested and demonstrated superior performance on three real-world datasets when compared to baseline methods.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness of type $B$ arises from the expression ${\rm tr} (X^2 Y - X Y^2) = {\rm tr} (X Y - X^2) + {\rm tr} (X Y^2 - X^2 Y)$, implying the relative error of the infinitesimal formula is $O(N^{-2})$. Consequently, the expected asymptotic conditional freeness of type $B$ holds with an error of $O(N^{-2})$. Furthermore, the infinitesimal formula and expected asymptotic conditional freeness of type $B$ can be extended to randomly perturbed matrices with independent entries.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that the primary source of isospin breaking arises from transition matrix $T$ and not from the final state. In regard to the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, it is established that it has a substantial impact on both branching fractions and spectral distribution. Specifically, when comparing the spectral distributions of $\gamma \pi^0$ and $\pi^0 \pi^0$, the latter exhibits a much more pronounced scalar component, primarily as a result of the $f_0(980)-a_0(980)$ mixing. Additionally, while the isospin breaking affects the spectral distribution, it has a minimal impact on the branching fractions. Our study also draws attention to the significance of non-resonant components in both decay reactions, particularly for regions below 1 GeV, where non-resonant $\pi^0 \eta$ dominates over all other contributions.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, while b) a field tracker captures images of the science target; c) a pupil imager re-images the telescope's pupil, and d) an aberration tracker captures images of a Shack-Hartmann sensor. The camera's detector images are analyzed using dedicated software to determine beam stabilization parameters, every 0.7 seconds. The obtained parameters are then applied to a) adjust the GRAVITY instrument to align with VLTI; b) actively stabilize the telescope's pupil and field of view; c) perform defocus correction, as well as various engineering tasks. The camera has successfully transitioned into operational use, with data reduction and on-sky characterization results having been documented.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with a limited set of supplier doubling dimension values and a specified number of anomalies. Conversely, for the more constrained Capacitated $k$-Center issue - a subset of CkSwO, with no additional costs and reduced supplier capacity - we demonstrate that achieving an approximate solution when dealing with highway dimension-based graphs is computationally challenging, even for a specific parameter range (with log n obstacles). Notably, while we know that logistic factor-based schemes exist for doubling dimension graphs, we prove that such factors cannot adequately account for highway dimension-based graphs, thus highlighting the distinction between these two dimension concepts.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper follows up on [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17] by refining those results in two key ways: introducing a new evaluation bound with reduced dependence on system parameters, and incorporating an early termination mechanism to prevent unnecessary computations arising from overestimating the system parameters or the error bound, both of which were concepts introduced in [Cabay, Proc. SYMSAC'71].

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of a particular electromagnetic mode in a cavity prevents it from splitting into two distinct emission channels. As a result, a protected emission channel exists for each possible photon number in the cavity, occurring at a frequency that varies linearly with it. This phenomenon can be observed using a pair of identical two-level systems as both emitters and detectors. The protection of the cavity's symmetry mode from splitting strongly affects its interaction with the cavity's eigenmodes, leading to a unique emission spectrum. Additionally, we illustrate that this protection can be partially lifted if the cavity's symmetry mode is not perfectly parity symmetric. The predicted effects are relevant to the study of cavity QED and can be easily replicated in small-scale experiments using existing technology.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored.
