This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. At its core lies the comparison of sequential data segments. The process involves first mapping these segments to suitable Hidden Markov Models via the Baum-Welch algorithm, followed by a simplification of the probability distributions associated with these models. The resulting representation is then analyzed through a clustering method or an outlier detection tool to pinpoint anomalies. Notably, the use of Hidden Markov Models could be replaced by alternative models, such as dynamic Bayesian networks, without affecting the overall method. The proposed algorithm operates in an unsupervised setting, eliminating the need for manual data labeling. The feasibility of this method is demonstrated through its application to simulated and real-world log data.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. Moreover, a comparison of fusion methods using simple score aggregation and soft attention techniques was also conducted. Experimental results obtained on the SpeakingFaces dataset showed that a multi-aspect verification system outperforms unimodal and bimodal approaches by significant margins, both in noise-free and noise-present scenarios. To promote research in the area and guarantee replicability of this research, our source code, pre-trained models, and dataset preprocessed for analysis were made freely accessible on our GitHub repository.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by appending existing examples to create new instances. We've found this approach to be both simple and cost-effective in boosting the performance of pre-optimized Transformer and Conformer models. Specifically, enhancements of up to 2.83 WER and 6.87 WER are seen in the LibriSpeech-960h test sets, and even higher when models were combined with fusion. Moreover, improvements of as much as 0.9 WER are recorded on the CoVoST-2 for several non-English languages following this training methodology. Notably, results indicate the magnitude of gain largely correlates with the size of initial training data. It is observed that our augmentation method can function effectively even when not utilizing speaker information. We've also demonstrated its effectiveness in translating spoken content into other languages by using this approach on multiple datasets, including speech translation tasks.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis.

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem for an efficient trade-off between utility and privacy.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough at 88 au that straddled multiple Keplerian velocity profiles related to a planet candidate and two companion candidates.
We observed that CO abundance differed significantly in the peak and trough regions.
However, we discovered that taking gas removal and chemical changes into account did not substantially alter the predicted CO abundance when compared with observations of $^{13}$C$^{16}$O.
Ultimately, we could not conclude whether the gas substructures in AS 209 were caused by gas voids or chemical voids.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint on state space. This builds upon an initial study by the same author, which was limited by incorrect assumptions regarding the growth rate of the drift vector field. We overcome this issue by introducing a more plausible assumption about the vector field's growth rate. This research enables the application of existing techniques for solving mean field games, while also highlighting potential issues arising from different growth rate assumptions.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led researchers to a phenomenon, dubbed "stellar strings," characterized by clumps of stars linked in the Milky Way galaxy's plane. Previous studies of these "strings" revealed a regular pattern of substructures within them, sparking speculation about their origin. In contrast, we conducted a more comprehensive examination of these "strings" in the Gaia data and our results contradict this earlier conclusion. By utilizing machine learning to map the sky, we discovered that the alleged "strings" actually comprise multiple, distinct structures overlapping in the sky, rather than continuous threads of stars. Consequently, the notion of a uniform pattern of substructures within these "strings" is no longer valid. Furthermore, we found that the "N-shapes" of these structures were largely the result of a prior filtering process, eliminating stars in the outer parts of the galaxy, thus leaving the core of these stars and creating the appearance of an 'N' shape when viewed in the sky. Additionally, our analysis revealed that the density of stars in the alleged "strings" decreases towards the galaxy's center, suggesting that these structures are actually a result of the limited field of view of the Gaia survey, obscuring the true appearance of the stellar distribution in the sky.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like color, style, and texture. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward combination of attributes and styles, resulting in poor performance when confronted with diverse, avant-garde fashion ensembles. We introduce the concept of visual incompatibility as a more effective approach and introduce the VICTOR network, a cutting-edge transformer model, to visually identify incompatibilities in outfits. The key distinction is the use of contrastive pre-training with a focus on understanding attribute relationships, as well as style nuances through fashion-specific pre-training. The incorporation of contrastive objectives empowers the network to learn visual attributes and relationships more effectively. We demonstrate the VICTOR's superiority over existing methods on two benchmark output datasets, achieving impressive performance gains of 78% and 66%. Additionally, our findings show that VICTOR's incompatibility detection capabilities can be extended to other areas such as mismatched clothing and fashion forgery by training on paired datasets.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse methods to quantify specific quantum effects. It plays a pivotal role in optimizing their utility across various applications. The incorporation of radical quantum phenomena such as coherence, entanglement, and nonclassicality has enabled their application in real-world contexts. The theoretical framework of quantum resource theory categorizes quantum states into 'free' and'resource' sets. Operations associated with free states emerge naturally from the system's constraints, whereas resource theories aim to discover and harness the potential within the restricted set. Recent breakthroughs in the field of standard harmonic oscillator quantum states have sparked rapid growth and advancements in the generalized quantum optical framework. The incorporation of contemporary ideas such as nonlinearity, non-Hermitian theories, and $q$-deformed bosonic systems aims to achieve elevated objectives in the field of quantum information. This article reviews recent developments in the resource theories of generalized quantum optical states and their applications in the realm of quantum information.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When the particles reassemble, the structure of the cracks follows a specific pattern. The speed at which the cracks form is determined by a balance between two forces, one of which is driven by pressure and the other by surface tension. The ratio of these speeds allows us to predict when the cracks will change from being shallow to being deep, resulting in an irregular raft structure. Furthermore, we find that the maximum force a crack can withstand before splitting the raft increases as the surface tension of the surrounding fluid grows.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of the heavy and light hole bands, resulting in a reduced hole mass along the compression axis. Consequently, our calculations indicate that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ boosts its room temperature hole mobility by 50% and 260%, respectively, when compared to strain-free GaN. Furthermore, our study analyzed the strain mobility correlations, allowing for the incorporation of these results into a existing model for GaN hole mobility.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-TD, a policy iteration algorithm that converges at a faster rate than previous methods.  The results of our experiments on an underwater robot platform match the accuracy of completely informed agents, while also outperforming previous sparse methods in terms of prediction and policy iteration performance.  Additionally, our approach excels at generalization tasks, such as navigating through wave-generated noise.  A detailed code implementation is available at https://github.com/joaosilva/spgp_td.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish a decomposition of $P$ into a finite sum of linear operators and show that each component can be estimated consistently using kernel methods. We have provided a detailed examination of the operator $P$ and its approximations, which can be applied to various nonparametric regression techniques including conditional probability estimation, regression estimation, and dynamic modeling.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated properties. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and provide a formula reminiscent of the Dobinski-like formula.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. SpliMe is informed by the splittable model concept and is compatible with a variety of static knowledge graph embedding algorithms. We conduct experiments on KILT's knowledge graph benchmark, which includes a dataset derived from DBpedia, and another from the DREAM challenge, which includes a dataset derived from BioASQ. We find that SpliMe's ability to analyze temporal patterns and generate temporal knowledge graph embeddings enables it to outperform existing static models and many temporal models.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for ongoing research regarding infinite graphs and their associated C*-algebras. Moreover, this note specifically explores insplits and outsplits as key examples of strong shift equivalences, demonstrating that these equivalences lead to Morita equivalences that maintain consistency across various weighted gauge actions. Consequently, a question is raised about whether strong shift equivalence can be expressed as a product of insplits and outsplits.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link size of X is O(log |X|). The basis of this algorithm is rooted in Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne's groups from 2005 that created the first discovered high dimensional expanders.

Incorporating our methods also reveals a novel sparsification algorithm for high dimensional expanders, maintaining its key local spectral characteristics, offering an area of independent interest.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. However, when the representation is $p$-irregular, things become more intricate as regular submodules are categorized by a flag variety, resulting in an abundance of choices that involve continuous parameters. Despite these complications, our analysis in select examples highlights how Hida theory and eigencurve geometry can facilitate the identification of a limited set of choices that possess notable arithmetic and'mixed-motivic' significance.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
model to leverage the atoms' sensitivity while minimizing the impact of noise 
without requiring the resolution of complex mathematical equations. In a key 
test, our Rydberg-deep learning system has enabled the direct extraction of 
encoded information from frequency-division multiplexed (FDM) signals, marking 
an important breakthrough in this field, and holding the potential to 
revolutionize the sensing and communication capabilities of Rydberg-based MW 
technology.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with other spiral galaxies reveals that UGC 8839 holds the record for the farthest hinge of its disk. In this research, we examine whether a gas loss episode, induced by interaction with a companion galaxy, explains the peculiar morphology and low star formation rate of UGC 8839's disk. However, since the companion galaxy is not noticeably interacting with UGC 8839, we assume that it was involved in a past collision that led to the gas loss. Consequently, a low-density disk formed, leading to the distinct star formation pattern observed in the outer region of UGC 8839. Additionally, we identify three distinct phases in the gas loss process, supported by N-body simulations, each resulting in the development of a hyper-stable disk. A comprehensive analysis including the stellar mass distribution, the fraction of dark matter, the stellar initial mass function, the disk's stability, and the internal dynamics of UGC 8839 are presented.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere, spanning between 120 and 190~km in altitude, is monitored. This observation sheds light on the effects of gravity waves (GWs), allowing scientists to analyze the behavior of GWs in the upper atmosphere under isothermal conditions and understand the role that the atmospheric background temperature plays in the propagation of GWs. Data obtained from past missions including the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, in combination with the new MAVEN findings, reveal an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the atmospheric background temperature, primarily found in the ODY mission's data collected over polar regions, rather than in the MGS and MRO datasets. Conversely, MRO's observations of the upper Martian atmosphere's behavior exhibit an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the Brunt-V\"{a}is\"{a}l\"{a} frequency. It is found that, in the atmospheric layer extending between 100 and 120~km in altitude, GW-induced density disturbances no longer correlate with temperature, instead aligning with atmospheric stability, whereas, in the three datasets collected by MGS, MRO, and ODY at non-polar latitudes, the intensity of the observed gravity waves does not correlate with temperature stability, instead pointing towards the role that the sources

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. As the LHC's energy threshold for photon-induced reactions approaches its current limit, further studies are required to expand our understanding of the nuclear photon structure. The ALICE experiment has made history by becoming the first to document J/psi production in Pb-Pb ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV, thanks to an analysis of the detector's inner tracking system. By examining in-flight J/psi decays across the entire LHC beam pipe, researchers gained insight into the photon flux, nuclear interactions, and the photon structure of the nucleus, all within a limited energy range.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample a single second of audio. We introduce a new model, called VisSaliency, that prioritizes the most influential visual elements to reduce the training data requirements and decrease sampling times. Our method is data-driven and learns the importance of different visual features by analyzing correlations between sound and vision datasets. By focusing on the most critical elements, VisSaliency streamlines the audio synthesis process, enabling fast, visual-based sound generation without the need for explicit condition response maps. It achieves notable advancements in both efficiency and quality compared to previous techniques.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, and speech recognition. Nonetheless, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex and computationally intensive due to the high dimensionality of hidden states. A notable achievement was made by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in addressing this challenge through the development of the back-propagation through time algorithm, presenting an updated version with a clearer explanation and simplified implementation.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility.' A fundamental analysis reveals that any situation involving limited resources, restricted information, and uncertain outcomes yields an 'economic irreversibility,' arguing that a typical pandemic scenario fits this category. Consequently, adopting timely moderate measures often provides the optimal solution to this complex problem.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, emphasizing the combinatorial aspect. A key example serves to illustrate the connections between these fields, namely the study of arrangements in projective space, specifically a specific variant of configuration spaces known as $r$-secant varieties of codimension $2$.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, characterized by a triangular antiferromagnetic structure. The generation of electrical resistance upon applying magnetic fields stems from the creation of a spin-symmetry breaking state with an ordered wavevector that matches the Bragg planes of the material's crystal structure, $k_{u} = k_{x}, k_{y} = 2k_{x}$, which triggers anomalous Hall behavior. Initial laboratory pressings to 1.6 GPa diminish this effect. Subsequent high-pressure experiments employing a diamond anvil cell revealed that increasing pressure up to 2.3 GPa results in the complete suppression of the anomalous Hall effect. X-ray diffraction and spectroscopy measurements showed that this phenomenon is attributed to a pressure-driven transformation of the material's interior structure, promoting a 120-degree ordering that eliminates the $k_{u}$-dependent amplitude in the spin structure and thus abolishes the anomalous Hall effect.

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it.  In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts.  This document serves
as an introduction to RE, providing an in-depth analysis of RE's fundamental concepts,
alongside an overview of recent developments in its application through machine learning
based methods, particularly deep neural networks.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented in traditional graph format. To address this issue, we develop a supervised hypergraph reconstruction framework aimed at capturing the underlying hypergraph structure from its graph representation. Given that hypergraph composition is inherently specified through inclusive relationships between node subsets, we establish a mathematical framework for expressing these inclusions between subsets of nodes, then apply a general machine learning approach to preserve the original hypergraph's class distinctions. Our proposed framework, incorporating established machine learning techniques, is flexible and allows for the incorporation of additional problem-specific constraints. We evaluate its effectiveness through experiments on two publicly available datasets, comparing two established graph reconstruction methods alongside our hypergraph reconstruction approach.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to be familiar with both normal anatomy and the detection of anomalies.
Current medical image analysis systems lack the knowledge of anatomical structure
appearance due to difficulty in collecting annotated data, thus restricting their
capability to narrow expertise areas, like diagnosing specific conditions. Our
research addresses this gap by incorporating human anatomy and allowing the
connection between report content and corresponding image content. To utilize
anatomical information, we introduce an advanced system to gather and integrate
human body structures from CT scans and demonstrate its application in enhancing
automated report understanding. Our experiments show that incorporating anatomical
information significantly improves the performance on report generation and
question-answering tasks. Additionally, our method exhibits versatile capabilities,
as demonstrated on multiple datasets across distinct procedures, utilizing both
chest X-rays and radiographs. Our data and model are publicly available for
limited access due to privacy concerns at https://www.4ai.org/anatomy/.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, and here we found support for the hypothesis that such errors would indeed fall within these bounds during periods of observed stability.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time stages. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific initial conditions of the KPZ equation, allowing for further generalization to other initial conditions.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers investigate properties of the solar wind's V_{nlos} component. They employ the first step of the Hall permission technique to analyze the solar wind's V_{nlos}^2/3 time series across various frequencies. Associated with the solar wind's low frequency fluctuations, researchers discover modulations in the solar wind's V_{nlos} component at around the V_{nlos}^2/3 ~ f_{pe}^2/3 threshold, suggesting the impact of ion acoustic fluctuations. Conversely, within the solar wind's high frequency range, researchers discover modulations in the solar wind's V_{nlos} component at around the V_{nlos}^2/3 ~ 4f_{pi}/3 threshold, suggesting the penetration of electron scale turbulence. Statistical analyses indicate the solar wind's V_{nlos} component exhibits similar properties across multiple spacecraft. Researchers investigate the variations in the solar wind's V_{nlos} component based upon interplanetary scintillation data and the fast plasma investigation's electron density measurements.

In SASE FELs, short pulse durations are restricted by the coherence time and the plasma undulator bandwidth.  To overcome these limitations, a modified chirp-taper scheme has been introduced.  This modified scheme incorporates an acousto-optic modulator and a defocusing solenoid magnet in the standard tapering process.  Numerical simulations have demonstrated the efficacy of this scheme in the XUV and soft X-ray wavelength ranges.  A specific example in the NLCXUV FEL showed that it enabled the creation of 30 attosecond pulses with a 2.6 nm wavelength, whereas the standard tapering process yielded a 220 fs pulse with the same wavelength.  Furthermore, this scheme demonstrated a substantial increase in pulse peak power from 0.3 to 30 GW during the same example.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity and diffusivity. By combining fourier series and asymptotic expansions, the study analyzes the boundary layer development in a turbulent water and salt-solution flow, comparing it to laminar flow for a smooth surface scenario. The investigation considers both smooth and rough surfaces, calculating the boundary layer solutions using both matching and physical optics methods. The study computes the drag experienced by an object immersed in the flow, comparing the results for turbulent and laminar flow scenarios.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. Ultimately, the sparse matrix derived from low-rank decomposition is de-noised through thresholding to pinpoint defect locations. Experimental findings demonstrate the proposed method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment's response to its actions. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices and select the most beneficial course of action. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization capabilities, outperforming current state-of-the-art models by at least 10% according to AI2-THOR evaluations. Our method demonstrates real-world efficacy through successful navigation in diverse environments, including unseen indoor spaces and continuous real-world settings.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, we find that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to ensure that the mass remains non-negative. Additionally, we determine the maximum mass loss rate per unit frequency interval that an infinite mass black hole can experience. This research utilizes advanced mathematical techniques to analyze a complex differential equation related to mass asymptotics.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters with lifetimes extending to the current age of the universe. These events will create mergers producing 10-500 times more energy than GW150914. Our predictions state that between the first 3 minutes after the Big Bang and the formation of galactic nuclei, 12-50 percent of Population III binary remnants will undergo a merger within a nuclear star cluster, and the most massive of these mergers will transmit gravitational waves in the range of 10^-2 to 1 Hz that will be detectable by future gravitational wave observatories with sensitivity similar to that of LISA.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly powered by the $\omega$ meson. The sequence of events involves the $\omega$ being created in the $X(3872)$'s decay and subsequently decaying into $J/\psi \gamma$, which combines with a nearby $\pi$ to form the final state. The second decay, $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$, has two sub-decays: one powered by the $\rho$ meson and the other by the $\omega$ meson. The team used form factors based on both Lattice QCD and QCD sum rules to complete the calculations. The results indicate that both decays receive contributions from both mesons, and the relative strength of the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons needs to be determined experimentally to fully understand the $X(3872)$'s transition between its ground state and the virtual $\rho$ or $\omega$ meson states. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ process is predicted to occur more frequently than the $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ process does. The study

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a versatile platform for assessing virtual agents' ability to process and generate text. Despite their potential, they have been hindered by low speeds of 10-100 actions per second. This limitation has forced researchers to choose between conducting a large number of experiments or the in-depth study of a single game. Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized text game engine capable of achieving one million actions per second. This speed enables the development of extensive virtual worlds, where agents can learn and adapt at an unprecedented level. Our investigation compares the computational costs of traditional text game methods and discovers that they can be improved by up to 100 times through simple yet effective techniques. Our research further combines these optimizations with a technique for dynamically generating texts, resulting in a virtual world that can process one million actions per second. TextWorldExpress, along with its source code, is now available at https://github.com/TextWorld/TextWorldExpress.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. In cases of defects, this shift occurs along closed paths in real space, with both instances characterized by non-trivial spin connections. This approach is utilized to determine the spin connections of three-dimensional Topological Insulators containing topological defects. The edge dislocation on the surface of a Topological Insulator generates a spin connection controlled by torsion, allowing electrons to move in confined circular areas and two-dimensional regions. The edge dislocations break parity symmetry, producing a current measured by the in-plane spin component on the surface, with this current accompanied by a tunneling density of states calculation for edge dislocations.

Consider the scenario where $p$ lies between 1 and infinity, $
u$ ranges between 0.5 and infinity, and $\mathcal{S}_
u$ denotes the set of non-zero vectors in 2D space with a polar angle smaller than $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$. We introduce $R > 0$, and $\omega_p(x)$ as the p-harmonic measure of $\partial B(0,R) \cap \mathcal{S}_
u$ at point $x$, relative to the ball $B(0,R)\cap \mathcal{S}_
u$. We show that for some constant $C$, the function $\omega_p(x)$ satisfies a specific inequality with respect to the exponent $k(
u,p)$, where the exponent depends on both $
u$ and $p$, and use this result to derive similar estimates for general $p$-harmonic functions in sectors. We also provide a detailed table showing the exact values of the exponent $k(
u,p)$ for specific cases where $p$ varies between 1 and infinity.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and tracking data, enabling efficient integration into a single framework. However, generating these ellipsoids from sparse optical data is challenging, and the typical approach of forming full matrices leads to computationally expensive calculations. In response, we have developed a more practical method for calculating manipulability ellipsoids using the information tensor, which we use to create a corresponding optimization problem. To address the issue of domain adaptation in robotics, our new method is combined with a transportation approach and the Manifold-ICP (Idea Connection Process) algorithm. The transportation approach helps to bridge the disparity in sparse corotation angles between the source and target domains, while Manifold-ICP accounts for the continuity of geometric structures in the target domain's point cloud. Experimental results show that the fusion of our new method, transportation approach, and Manifold-ICP successfully performs domain adaptation for manipulating objects with a robotic arm.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency.

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, in-the-wild video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered using smartphones. The method leverages video constraints to reduce the complex object pose space and employs a novel regression technique that synchronizes the predicted poses with the underlying video content. The approach is flexible, allowing the integration of conventional image-based models through a straightforward two-stage training process. When applied to standard datasets, the method significantly enhances model performance and demonstrates robustness in challenging real-world video scenarios.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can determine a user's response to counterarguments on the COVID-19 vaccine. This framework leverages dialogue systems to simulate counterarguments and measures the similarity between the simulated conversation and actual user comments as an indicator of adoption or rejection of the counterargument. Experimental results using Twitter data confirm the effectiveness of this framework in accurately predicting user responses to counterarguments.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. Our findings demonstrate that by manipulating the waveform of the driving laser pulse via its relative phase and carrier-envelope phase, it's possible to exert fine-grained control over attosecond pulse characteristics. This innovation not only amplifies experimental possibilities in the realm of attosecond science, but also paves the way for a highly sophisticated, coherent manipulation of free-electron paths.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data that is no longer accurate. This involves accounting for potential companions that can create recurring periods in time shifts. A study discovered a low probability (0.00005%) of detecting new companions using eclipse time shifts. Researchers analyzed data on Algol ($\beta$ Persei) and found tentative signs of up to five additional companion candidates, which are believed to have orbital periods ranging from 1.863 to 219 years. These candidates are thought to have mass ratios approximately between 0.093 and 0.168 and are likely to be bound to the primary star. Further research is needed to confirm these companion candidates through various methods, including direct imaging and spectroscopy.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adjustable nodal distribution method and a memory mechanism. We then conduct experiments on both linear and nonlinear PDEs, evaluating its accuracy and efficiency relative to traditional sampling methods.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. Our analysis also shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, which in turn affects the device's drain current and variability due to the domain period. We also investigated how the domain wall's soft or hard state transition influences the device's electrical properties and transport. Our simulations are verified through both experimental data and phase-field modeling.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook the unique technical characteristics of individual ecosystems, hindering direct applicability of security governance strategies to Cargo. To address this disparity, this research employs knowledge graph techniques to construct a dependency vulnerability graph for Cargo and presents an innovative algorithm to identify vulnerability dissemination paths and scope. By conducting a comprehensive empirical study on Cargo's ecosystem, this research investigates vulnerability traits, propagation extent, and factors influencing vulnerability dissemination, revealing that Cargo's security vulnerabilities primarily stem from memory-related issues. Notably, 18% of libraries still harbor vulnerabilities even after updating to the latest version, while 19.78% of Cargo's ecosystem versions are affected by propagated vulnerabilities. This study's findings offer actionable insights for Cargo administrators, developers, and library owners to enhance ecosystem security and presents new concepts for bolstering Cargo's overall security posture.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results apply universally, imposing minimal restrictions on noise conditions. A critical factor in this study is the authors' and T. Zhang's previously established criteria for irreducibility in stochastic equations with jump noises. This proof is then utilized to demonstrate ergodic behavior in stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations and includes scenarios of weak dissipation with jump degenerate noise.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational cost, with a significant reduction in model complexity.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental results demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and accelerated inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy for point cloud learning. The source code will be publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ofsoundof/EfficientGCN.git.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, making our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same category and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes preparing the optics, coating the first slicer, crafting the mounts, and writing the software, all aiming to enhance IMACS's functionality by facilitating the efficient examination of expansive astronomical objects like nebulae and galaxies.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Earth. However, our analysis reveals two exceptions, the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 planets, which would likely develop cores significantly smaller than Earth due to oxidation. Furthermore, we examined the potential for water in these exoplanets, discovering that only a few could harbour habitable environments analogous to Earth's, primarily as a result of their host stars' differing metallicities. This study stresses the importance of considering both elemental composition and volatile depletion when modelling terrestrial planets around various types of stars.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) where 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. Under certain conditions, specifically when n is greater than or equal to the sum of i and j, and when the size of the alphabet is 3 or greater, we identify the functions with minimum possible support and establish a characterization for those with such a minimum. In scenarios where n is less than the sum of i and j, but with a sufficiently large alphabet size of at least 4, we identify similar properties of functions. In particular, we establish a characterization for the functions within the eigenspace U_i(n,q) with minimum possible support in several specific scenarios.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing web access to existing models. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is developed to tackle both forward and inverse problems governed by partial differential equations. To illustrate the utility and potential benefits of this framework, uncertainty quantification is applied to solve a crucial problem in nuclear reactor core modeling critical to ensuring public safety. This work showcases the application of NNs in a context where their traditional counterparts are often unfeasible, offering promising implications for science and engineering practitioners.

We are investigating quantum group analogues of the free group factors' radial subalgebras, specifically those of class functions, within the context of compact quantum groups. We found that the algebras of class functions for the free orthogonal quantum groups cannot be maximally abundant *-subalgebras (MASAs) under certain conditions. Central tendencies of these algebras were also examined, leading to conclusions about their operator system isomorphisms and monotonic isomorphisms, as well as the existence of abundant ideals within these algebras.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of methods with local quadratic contraction rates and reduced computational requirements, was introduced, specifically applied to mean-field MDPs and ultimately led to its application in general MDPs via mean-field approximation. However, its applicability to general MMDPs relies heavily on the specification of a compact set of states. In this paper, we remove this restriction by adapting inexact policy iteration to general MMDPs without the need for an a priori defined state compact set. Moreover, we further modify it to fit the matrix representation of MMDPs and numerically verify its superiority over regular policy iteration using the GMRES algorithm in experiments.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently tackle the computational challenge, researchers transformed the state-space problem into a multiple contour estimation issue and proposed a non-parametric approach to tackle it. An initial experiment tested the efficiency of the proposed method, followed by an analysis of its performance and shortcomings. Ultimately, researchers demonstrated that the newly developed technique results in minimal errors when compared to the computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo method.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust measure of model accuracy. These algorithms can learn robust models capable of withstanding perturbations of moderate size. In addition, we establish a new set of conditions that ensure the existence of learning algorithms capable of handling random example exposure, expanding upon the initial distribution-free learning results presented in Bousquet and Raghavan (2000).
The relationship between local queries and robust learning is further explored in this work, and we provide evidence suggesting that certain concepts are impossible to learn robustly when using local queries, depending on the specific model evaluation metric employed.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the LHC, operating at a proton-proton center of mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined across the entire fragmentation phase, and also within two parts, relative to the leading photon direction. By pairing with a lead lead collision at either zero or forward rapidity, modifications to the fragmentation functions were identified, and found to increase the ratio of underlying fragmentation functions in the forward to the unmodified range by as much as 11.2% at 40% of the fragmentation distance. Various interpretations based on theoretical models have been considered.
