Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for the object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a very low temperature consistent with the Y dwarf spectrum and a large radius. Moreover, the object possesses color indices not in line with standard binary object spectra, and is instead thought to be a solitary object with a unique composition featuring elevated carbon and water content. Data from the object's photometry, along with temperature measurements from ALMA and IGRIN data, have indicated a temperature of 405K and a mass of approximately 3.6 x 10^-2 M_sun, suggesting the object is in the midst of transitioning from the main sequence to the white dwarf phase. The object's distance is estimated to be around 17-20 pc and is thought to be an ultra-cool dwarf lying in the solar neighborhood, or possibly the remnant of a brown dwarf that has lost its outer layers in a close celestial collision.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and the initial stages of 3D printed materials. The results indicated that firing temperatures significantly impacted both the internal structures and the mechanical properties of these simulants. The best firing temperature was found to be around 1100 C, which resulted in a solid internal structure and optimal mechanical properties, specifically tensile and compressive strengths of 0.98 MPa and 5.40 MPa for Martian simulants and 0.82 MPa and 1.63 MPa for Lunar simulants. The contraction of these materials followed a predictable pattern, with firing temperature being the primary influencing factor. Additionally, Lunar simulants contracted more than Martian ones, with some variations. Based on these findings, it is possible to create structural components using 3D printing and traditional building methods with materials derived from Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, which could be used to construct habitats and other infrastructure on other planets.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\gamma$-band bracket wavelength could improve SFR predictions by incorporating a feature that is less influenced by dust, which in turn would require fewer assumptions about dust calibration.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we classify the braided auto-equivalences of the local modules in the category given by the tensor product of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$ and the type II quantum subgroups, specifically identifying twenty distinct orthonormal solutions to the braided auto-equivalence equivariance condition, each corresponding to a substantial type II subgroup. Furthermore, we establish an isomorphism between the category consisting of the type II subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$ and a subcategory consisting of the categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{\tilde{r}},k) \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_{2}$. Notably, we demonstrate that the twenty distinct orbits described earlier correspond to the type II quantum subgroups of categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{\tilde{r}},k)$. In the follow-up paper, we intend to elaborate on the central results of this study, specifically classifying parallel weight modules for each of the twenty orbits, and presenting examples corresponding to four of these orbits.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field.

This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based information extraction method is applied to break down the labeled data. Following this process, two machine learning models are developed - the first is a binary classifier leveraging a hybrid Deep Neural Network and Random Forest to detect writing activities, and the second is a Deep Neural Network integrating convolutional and recurrent layers for single-character classification. Although the proposed approach demonstrates satisfactory accuracy and performance in the challenge evaluation simulation with an average Levensthein Distance of 8, its overall efficiency and real-time capabilities still require improvement.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech.

Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data from various sources, various modifications to the fundamental single species occupancy model have been introduced. However, creating high-performance software that can analyze large spatial data sets is still a developing field. A newly developed package, spOccupancy for R, is designed to fit single, multiple species, and combined occupancy models that are sensitive to spatial relationships. Utilizing a Bayesian approach with Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and Gaussian Process neighbor techniques, this package enables efficient model computation even for extensive datasets. spOccupancy provides intuitive functionalities for model fitting, evaluation, comparison, and interpretation, including features for simulating data, testing predictions, and making predictions on unseen sites and times. A detailed case study is presented to illustrate the package's capabilities, employing data collected from California's yellow-legged frog to estimate its overall occupancy, pairwise species occupancy relationships, and individual species occupancy coupled with spatial autocorrelation effects.

Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence. The Skincare project aimed to address this by creating an innovative diagnostic and decision support system in dermatology. It combined the capabilities of interactive machine learning with deep learning to enhance the skills of doctors and augment diagnostic capabilities, particularly in the identification of malignant skin lesions. A baseline model, trained using a large dermatology image dataset (ISIC), delivered outstanding results and demonstrated potential for widespread application, including support for both general practitioners and dermatologists. The project also focused on creating effective communication channels between humans and machines to facilitate machine learning. In essence, the Skincare project sought to integrate human intuition with artificial intelligence, a key component of future cognitive assistants in the medical sector.

To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training framework within our physically-parameterized network enabled the separation of intrinsic and extrinsic variability, eliminating the need for magnitude standardization models. The PAE was applied in several tasks to improve cosmological analyses, such as automatically detecting outliers, generating sample spectra consistent with data distribution, and resolving noisy inverse problems to estimate cosmological distances. Notably, we found three intrinsic model parameters yielded the best results, in line with existing research. The PAE achieved an optimal standardization of $0.091 \pm 0.010$ mag for our test sample of SNe Ia, reducing to $0.074 \pm 0.010$ mag when peculiar velocity contributions are removed. The model demonstrates a $2.4\sigma$ detection of Hubble constant deviations and indicates higher-than-expected magnitude standardization errors for high-z SNe Ia. The PAE source code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/georgestein/suPAErnova}{github.com/georgestein/suPAErnova}.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a gravitationally lensed star-forming galaxy. The outflow is visible in a specific OH+ absorption line, which was measured by the ALMA telescope at high spatial resolution. The data also include CO emission, dust, and stellar light. Analysis of the outflow shows that it has different properties than other elements within the galaxy. The mass of the outflow is estimated to be approximately 6.7 billion solar masses. The outflow's properties are best explained by a conical shape. Depending on the inclination angle, the outflow's rate of gas loss and kinetic energy could be quite high. This suggests that the outflow may impact the galaxy's star formation. The outflow may eventually be re-accreted back into the galaxy, but this would depend on various feedback mechanisms. The estimated gas depletion time in the galaxy is around 1-29 million years.

To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume containing heavy particles that sink more slowly than the plume moves, researchers used controlled experiments in a lab setting. The experiments focused on the effects of particle size, density, and the direction in which the particles move relative to the direction of the plume's movement. The results revealed a significant increase in the rate at which fluid moves into the plume when compared to the rate for pure water under similar conditions. The amount of increase varied based on the characteristics of the particles and the direction of their movement relative to the plume's direction. The experiments also showed that when the particles move in the same direction as the plume, a significant reduction in the rate at which fluid moves into the plume occurs. The obtained results are in line with previously developed theoretical concepts for particle-laden turbulent plumes.

Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and study various types of contagion models, considering both the stochastic individual-level model and the mean-field approximation. Numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the implications of these conditions and compare our findings to the results obtained using the traditional pairwise model.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors have led to the way for using spin in next-generation technology. Researchers are now seeking to harness the inherent properties of these materials to control the flow of electrical current with magnetic fields. Studying the magnetic properties at the most basic level is crucial for achieving this goal, and our study focuses on examining the magnetic properties of the bilayer of ferromagnetic chromium iodide. Using advanced computational techniques to determine the magnetic properties in an experimentally verified structure revealed a non-trivial spin pattern caused by the imbalance of magnetic fields in the layers. Additionally, a unique form of magnetic direction alteration is produced, which is not typically seen in standard magnetic materials and is a result of the uneven magnetic fields. Furthermore, applying an external electric field can control the direction of magnetic fields within the layers and thus the flow of electrical current, which is a result of the uneven magnetic fields and is a characteristic of a unique form of electrical-magnetic interaction.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in very slow rotators, including some satellitars. This study is the first to investigate how solar-type stars with this unique differential rotation transition to the magnetic phase of their life cycles. Using idealized simulations, it has been determined that, compared to the traditional rotational velocity profile, those with the anti-solar profile can support solutions suitable for observed star types, primarily involving small and slow rotating stars. These solutions indicate that star types with the anti-solar differential rotation transition to the magnetic phase tend to produce weaker and slower magnetic cycles.

Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. We present a K-fan deep model, featuring a K-branch architecture for handling multi-input, multi-output tasks efficiently. Each branch of the model can comprise multiple layers of neural networks. A shared representation is learned in a discriminative manner to tackle multiple tasks. We propose two optimization methods tailored to joint visual restoration and object recognition tasks. Model parameters are initially estimated through maximum joint distribution and then fine-tuned using backpropagation based on the specific task. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the model in utilizing multiple information sources to perform well across various competitive baselines.

The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the handling of spurious wake-ups triggered by condition variables. By streamlining the McMini model checking framework, the mechanism makes it possible to run McMini model checks in a distributed setting, leveraging a high-performance cluster of multiple GPUs.

The globally predominant messaging app, WhatsApp, boasts a distinct characteristic 
in its closed nature and user-friendly capabilities of transferring multimedia and
large-scale information sharing to groups, which often facilitates the rapid spread 
of anonymous, encrypted messages. However, during times of crisis, such as the COVID-19 
pandemic and elections, malicious activities involving misinformation have prompted 
concerns about the app's potential dangers. In response to these valid concerns held 
by public figures, users are left wondering whether limiting message forwarding could 
effectively counter misinformation dissemination. In this study, we assess the potential 
effectiveness of this solution by modeling user behavior, assessing the impact of limits 
on misinformation spread, and examining the influence of public awareness campaigns 
aimed at reducing belief in misinformation. Our findings indicate that implementing 
limits only delays the spread of misinformation, ultimately proving ineffective in the 
long term. Importantly, combining limits with awareness campaigns leads to only slight 
costs in terms of added time required for misinformation dissemination. Additionally, 
we identify specific features of malware spread and develop a dynamic policy model to 
determine the optimal time to implement limits on message forwarding.

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. This work aims to propose approximation methods that replace this frequency spectrum with simpler quantities and assess the asymptotic error associated with these approximations using central limit theorems. Finally, we apply this model through numerical analysis, focusing particularly on the relationship between one of the proposed approximations and Sabeti's Extended Haplotype Homozygosity measure.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial sounds made by humans as part of voice manipulation. While countermeasures for detecting voice manipulation have been developed, their performance significantly declines when dealing with artificial sounds. To overcome this issue, we introduce a novel attentive activation function called the attentive rectified linear unit and incorporate it into a deep neural network. This innovative mechanism enables the system to prioritize and focus on key characteristics of speech signals that are susceptible to manipulation. Our experimental results demonstrate that the system surpasses current state-of-the-art spoofing detection models by 97% in the speaker verification task and 99% in the speaker identification task. Additionally, the system exhibits an impressive 44% improvement in speaker verification performance with our proposed mechanism.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars, including the standard model scalars promoted to scalars by the supergravity mechanism, remain heavy compared to the Hubble scale during inflation.  This thesis presents several supergravity inflationary models, starting with an existing model modified to incorporate recent LHC findings and two new constructions, one from an $SO(6)$ gauge group and another from an $SU(3)$ group, showcasing the diversity of supergravity inflationary models.  Additionally, this thesis proposes a model of randomly generated supergravity scalar potentials, aiming to tackle the issue of landscape meta-physics in the context of supergravity by evaluating the likelihood of meeting the requirements for inflationary models and moduli stabilization through the combination of two distinct volumes within the landscape.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while adjusting the pump's intensity and frequency maintains nonreciprocity.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate how varying the length of L-shaped inductors influences their mode order, leveraging near-field terahertz spectroscopy to identify order transitions. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of terahertz scanning for characterizing quantum circuit building blocks at the nanoscale, enabling precise optimization of device performance and device-scale parameter mapping for quantum error correction and correction by mapping.

We are looking for infinite cardinals $\kappa$ that allow for a division of the real number line $\mathbb R$ into $\kappa$ unique Borel sets. The well-known Hausdorff solution indicates that $\aleph_1$ sets work in one instance. Our research shows, however, that the size range for these divisions can vary extensively, allowing a specific set of natural numbers $A$ with values 0 and 1 included to dictate when $\aleph_n$ sets work in a specific forcing extension. The study is expanded to closed sets and similar results found that show uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ sizes for these divisions are fairly arbitrary.

In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - both CTA and SRT traders achieved higher profits in combined markets compared to markets with only CTA traders. Furthermore, a detailed analysis revealed that the benefits accrued to both CTA and SRT traders, implying a symbiotic relationship between these market participants.

Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Generally, identification of the application protocol is based on specific characteristics, such as port numbers, static settings, or simple connections. However, detecting the application protocol through these methods is insufficient, as it results in incorrect or ambiguous conclusions regarding unknown or spoofed traffic. To address this, researchers have created and refined rules for identifying the application protocol based on various traffic patterns. Specifically, rules related to transport-layer protocols have shown considerable potential in this regard. This study aims to enhance the capability of identifying the application protocol by exploring the feasibility of deploying deep learning methods on top of existing transport-layer protocol classification rules. A novel approach using a deep neural network is proposed to dynamically identify the application protocol within short packets. The results indicate that this method achieves superior accuracy compared to existing rule-based methods and outperforms them by a significant margin in identifying the application protocol. Importantly, the proposed approach features fast query times, making it incredibly useful in high-performance network security monitoring systems.

Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The added capability to control coherent magnons enables new functionalities in magnonic devices, including reconfigurable logical circuits and stronger connections to other systems of degrees of freedom.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unseen data patterns on various devices challenge this methodology as they are not accessible to the central server or fellow users. In response, we suggest a unified system addressing the associated issues during federated learning. Our system is evaluated in two distinct settings - 1) when users conceal the new class labels, and 2) when users disclose this information, whereupon we simulate user data representations by comparing class similarities, and use clustering techniques to differentiate among them. Our system is capable of handling disparities among users' labels and models as well. Our framework is experimentally verified on two prominent applications: voice recognition and urban sound detection. It exhibits an average improvement in classification accuracy of around 4% on both platforms across multiple updates and different data patterns.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces operating within the sub-6 GHz frequency range where channel propagation isn't sparse. A high-performance, low-overhead estimation protocol has been developed to minimize reflection power loss without requiring on-off amplitude control. The proposed solution exploits a common structure within the system, significantly reducing pilot transmission overhead by decomposing the complex cascaded channel into separate user-specific and shared variables. The challenge of highly coupled estimation variables is overcome through the use of optimization-based estimation methods utilizing channel covariance. An alternating optimization algorithm has been developed to efficiently solve the resulting non-convex problem, with an efficient initialization technique ensuring a local optimal solution. The research shows that this approach offers considerable reductions in pilot overhead and reflection loss compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned.

Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this concept has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter can surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in performance, all while consuming even less storage space than these solutions. A variant of the xor filter, known as xor filter minimal, was also designed to take advantage of memory that is not divided into bytes, such as memory that is 4 or 8 bytes in size.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively.

A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the point at which the model's predictions reach a state of equilibrium. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by exponential moving averages and predicted prices derived from the model's calculations. To measure the difference between these two sets of prices, the approach employs the mean absolute difference, and the resulting metric is used to assess the state of the market.

This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-based testing to validate their local models, then submit verified models to the server for consolidation. We have mathematically demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach and conducted thorough experiments that showcase its advantages over existing federated learning methods.

We successfully adapted an end-to-end autonomous driving model trained in a simulated environment to navigate real-world roads. Our approach leverages image gradients within the model to incorporate spatial coherence, thus enabling the model to translate pixel movements into tangible road conditions. By incorporating this gradient information, the model's output became significantly more robust and capable of withstanding simulations' inherent inconsistencies. Furthermore, we refined the model through a self-correction protocol, incorporating real-world feedback not initially available during the initial training process. The outcomes demonstrate that incorporating gradient information enhances the model's real-world applicability while enabling continuous improvement with minimal, data-driven adjustments in real-world settings.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Furthermore, it proposes future research directions for tackling deepfake-related issues.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being inherently conflicting. Thermochemical recycling of carbon and nitrogen in the massive atmosphere of a temperate exoplanet typically produces CH4 and NH3, while a small atmosphere atop a liquid water ocean would contain CO2 and N2, with the presence of photochemically produced CO and CH4, and reduced NH3 due to dissolution in the ocean. These distinctive atmospheric compositions produce distinctive features in the planet's transmission spectrum, and multiple observations with the James Webb Space Telescope should enable differentiation between a small vs. massive atmosphere on temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets, including K2-18b, thereby facilitating a means to use current technology to estimate the mass of these atmospheres and assess their habitability potential.

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, similar to synaptic consolidation in animal memories. The model's learning efficiency and capacity have been rigorously evaluated, revealing exceptional performance compared to other spike-based sequence learning models, such as neural differential equations. Furthermore, our MPN model exhibits remarkable robustness to random disruptions in both binary and gray-scale binary neuron configurations. To illustrate its practical significance, a binary MPN model was utilized to learn and predict sequences of visual stimuli, a well-established task known as the 'bar-bucket task,' in insect olfactory system simulations. The binary MPN model offers a theoretically grounded approach to sequence learning in spiking neural networks, characterized by biological plausibility, efficiency, and capacity for learning complex temporal patterns in binary neuron networks.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research focused on tackling the OOV challenge.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating the difference between a solution that doesn't take uncertainty into account and its corresponding chaotic expansion, with a particular focus on proving continuity for this difference. This framework is then demonstrated with a numerical analysis using a specific mathematical example.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the cause of failure is essential. This work aims to develop an adaptive monitoring system capable of handling high-dimensional data in real-time, and also identifying potential failures. To achieve this, we've developed a sequential change detection and diagnosis approach based on Bayesian decision theory. The proposed method utilizes a unified statistical model to identify failures and isolate their source, and works in real-time by adapting to emerging failures and incorporating new data as it becomes available. The approach's efficiency is further enhanced by shrinkage estimation, and its performance is evaluated using synthetic and real-world data sets.

We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. By examining the ages, chemical compositions, and formation histories of thousands of stars in these systems, we have mapped their development over time, revealing a complex history for both galaxies. Approximately 7.2 billion years ago, GSE began forming stars, then experienced a starburst before falling into the Milky Way around 3.9 billion years ago. In contrast, Wukong/LMS-1 started forming stars around 10 billion years ago, stopped for about 7 billion years, and then experienced another starburst before merging with the Milky Way approximately 1 billion years ago. Comparing these findings to other galaxies of similar stellar masses, we have discovered that both GSE and Wukong/LMS-1 followed a similar pattern of star formation, despite their diverse environments. However, both galaxies's star formation patterns are distinct from more massive galaxies like the Milky Way. By analyzing the relationships between different chemical elements within these galaxies, we have identified possible issues with theoretical models that attempt to simulate galaxy formation, as these simulations predict different chemical patterns than what we observe in the galaxies.

Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills certain criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG} associated with an S[[G]]-module X. When X's constituents meet specific finiteness criteria, a homotopy orbit spectral sequence arises with an E2-term being the continuous homology of G, taking coefficients from the graded profinite \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}[[G]]-module \pi_*(X). This is demonstrated with an equivalence for certain conditions on G and Z: specifically, (Z[[G]])_{hG} is shown to be equivalent to Z in those scenarios, with supplementary methods for further investigation provided.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different industries found that selective labeling accelerates the labeling process by a significant margin - up to 8.7 times faster - without compromising on classification accuracy in the extraction of relevant document features.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices.  The feasibility of incorporating EuS, a ferromagnetic insulator, into a semiconductor as a means to achieve magnetic properties in a semiconductor material.  The interface's electronic structure, specifically band alignment, plays a vital role in utilizing the magnetic properties and understanding interactions at the interface.  Computational studies using density functional theory, based on different bonding configurations at the interface, have shown variations in band alignment and magnetic properties.  The findings indicate that the bonding configuration has a significant impact on the electronic properties of the EuS/InAs interface.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate the availability of significant computational resources. Previous attempts at improving efficiency involved increasing the network depth or adjusting the spatial dimensions of convolutional layers. Despite these advancements, the required computational power for training still surpassed the capabilities of a single GPU. To address this limitation, we present ClickTrain, a novel method that efficiently, accurately, and entirely trains CNNs on a single GPU without compromising accuracy. ClickTrain employs fine-grained pruning of both direct and cross weights within layers, combined with a strategy for adapting the pruned model into a deeper network through the reconnection of neurons. This innovative approach allows ClickTrain to outperform existing pruning techniques by achieving an impressive 4.5 to 6.6 times acceleration while requiring 0.0-0.4% additional computational resources, thereby enabling the end-to-end training of previously challenging ResNepts-50, 53, 54, 56 and 59 models on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO-Virgo data against a dataset consisting of binary black hole and binary neutron star events. The network achieves a 93 percent accuracy in distinguishing signals from background noise, and a 83 percent accuracy in classifying signals as either binary black hole or binary neutron star events.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been further confirmed using data from ground-based spectrographic equipment. Analysis of this data has shown that the exoplanet likely has a mass consistent with that of Jupiter. TOI-5542 is notable due to its relatively low metal content, which is unusual as it has a large amount of larger exoplanets. It is proposed that one possible explanations for this discrepancy is that the metal-enriched material that forms gas giant exoplanets is deficient in the vicinity of TOI-5542. Another possibility is that the exoplanet has undergone mass loss due to wind or other factors. The study provides more information about the properties of the exoplanet, which suggests it is composed primarily of rock and gas. The exoplanet, which is estimated to be about 3 billion years old, is thought to be an old warm Jupiter that could provide valuable insights into the evolution of these types of planets.

Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two primary techniques for solving CMDP involve formulating the problem as a linear programming and using dual decomposition. However, these approaches face difficulties due to issues with dual feasibility and convergence. Introducing a dual version of the primal-dual linear programming algorithm initially proposed by Yin and Jia resolves these issues, making it possible to achieve dual feasibility and converge to optimal solutions efficiently. This approach is examined in various CMDP scenarios with distinct limitations and demonstrates faster convergence rates overall.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols, like the square root symbol, can't be processed this way. What's more, handwritten mathematical symbols can look very similar, for example, handwritten zero and the Greek letter null. Given the numerous mathematical symbols, over 300 in total, a highly effective training dataset needed to be developed for the recognition system to work well. The study details the creation of an offline handwritten mathematical symbol recognizer, encompassing over 300 classes, achieved with a high accuracy of 97.6% utilizing a Siamese network paired with a contrastive loss function.

A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has a symplectic resolution with equivariant symplectic properties. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies are related to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the duality concept we introduced between a 7D black hole and superconformal quantum mechanics.

We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is surprisingly small, yet the latter's complex structure can lead to a lower overall infection rate. Unlike non-clustered networks, the presence of robust community structures in the network causes a phenomenon of'self-cleaning,' where disease outbreaks tend to be contained within specific regions. Specifically, the observation period is long enough to note the effects of which path an infected particle travels through the network and the order in which particles become infected. Ultimately, our research shows that networks with a mix of small and large community structures are more resilient than those composed of many isolated local clusters or a single large group.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method has numerous benefits, primarily expressed in the increased exploration of the policy space by leveraging a more accurate posterior approximation through HMC. Consequently, the Hamiltonian Policy significantly surpasses the traditional actor-critic model in numerous synthetic and real-world robotic control scenarios using only a small number of time steps.

It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, searching for these twin primes at the level of their respective generators makes practical sense. This paper introduces a novel strategy for verifying the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing a sieving approach to extract and analyze the twin prime pairs from a predefined set of generators. Using this framework, we can confidently state that the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ will eventually be verified as the number of analyzed generators approaches infinity. In fact, our studies have demonstrated that even when using a relatively small set of $\textbf{candidate generators}$, which grows at an approximately quadratic rate as the number of considered integers increases, the resulting pair count of twin primes exceeds the existing record set by Cheung Hung-yee. This breakthrough offers a new methodology that can be employed to validate the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ as the number of considered integers increases without limits.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. This work presents a novel indoor navigation system for low-cost mobile robots, utilizing a sonar sensor to gather data and a customized controller based on a layered architecture, combining reinforcement learning and rule-based methods to achieve efficient and real-time results. The system's performance is evaluated in an indoor environment with a dynamically changing terrain and compared to state-of-the-art techniques using a parameter called success rate metric. The findings reveal that the proposed system surpasses existing methods in terms of speed and reliability while maintaining real-time capabilities.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that has not been captured through gravitational binding to the planet. Information about Nereid's composition provides insight into the solar system's early development and its potential delivery of materials to the planets. Details about Nereid's surface composition are limited, attributed to the difficulty in obtaining detailed images of the poorly bound satellite. We carried out a thorough analysis of Nereid's low-resolution reflectance spectrum, combining it with constraints from thermal emission, to determine the spectral and physical properties of its surface ice mixtures. The laboratory simulations of Tholin and Tholins, accompanied by spectral modeling, enabled us to determine the fractions of water ice crystals and the presence of magmatic Tholin on Nereid's low-albedo areas. The combination of Nereid's bound albedo and deep reflectance spectrum, along with its thermal emission, enabled us to determine the size of its near-surface Tholin pool, suggesting the satellite's existence is accompanied by a magmatic event. The availability of Nereid's new low-resolution reflectance spectrum in the database of the Spacelink Planet database, along with its archival in the Spacelink Planet database, allows for future utilization of the data in modeling the satellite's physical parameters and its surface composition in the spectral range of 0.8-2.5 micrometers.

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2T_n(q)}$. Studies have proven that over the projective line based on $T_n(q)$, we find $(q+1)^{(n-1)}q^{\frac{3(n-1)(n-2)}{2}}$ affine planes of order $q$, where points and lines within such a plane satisfy specific submodule properties. These affine planes are ultimately shown to be extendable to a projective plane of order $q$, where free left ${^2T_n(q)}$-subspaces corresponding to its points meet certain criteria. Similar analyses have been conducted for the specific cases of $n = 3$ and $4$.

In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven through a novel application of Tukey-order with models, expanding upon an existing concept introduced by Vojtáš in 1991. By leveraging this notion, it can be shown that certain model properties can imply each other, thereby establishing key theorems related to random and Cohen reals within these models.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline pessimism solutions frequently result in suboptimal outcomes because they concentrate on the most unfavorable possibilities without considering the overall uncertainty. Our approach, unlike existing pessimism methods that rely on convex relaxations, directly optimizes for the most pessimistic scenario by taking the minimum of the discounted long-term costs across all possible treatment pathways. This black-box pessimism solution generalizes existing ideas and can be implemented using any Bayesian estimator. When combined with Bayesian policy optimization, the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art offline and online solutions in a diverse set of scenarios, according to simulations and a case study based on electronic health records.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. When restricting these relationships to subcategories of finitely generated modules with particular dimensions, previously established correspondences and dualities on tilting modules are reaffirmed. The implications of this relationship include demonstrating equivalences of derived categories of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules, as well as the invariance of certain algebraic invariants under tilting transformations.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of multi-band Hubbard models exhibiting exact pairing ground states across all symmetries. Through analytical computations, we discovered that many-electron excitations are governed by a simple effective Hamiltonian equivalent to that of non-interacting massless Dirac fermions moving through electromagnetic fields. We found the low-energy excitations to consist of linearly dispersing electron-like and hole-like states paired at the Fermi point, as well as bosonic modes carrying spin and orbital angular momentum. Our analysis indicates that a variety of electronic and bosonic excitations are observable in flat band superconductors through experimental methods such as ARPES and heat capacity measurements.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid.

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot easily be compared theoretically. To address this, we conduct an in-depth comparative analysis through simulation studies grounded in models for species distribution to evaluate their respective performances. 

This study has been accepted for publication in an upcoming publication titled "Innovations in multivariate statistical modelling: navigating theoretical and multidisciplinary domains," part of Springer Emerging Topics in Statistics and Biostatistics, edited by Ferreira, J., Bekker, A., Arashi, M., and Chen, D.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both channels and color dimensions. This structure's simplicity and efficacy enable efficient extraction and fusion of contextual information, leading to superior performance across various benchmark datasets, with results showcasing considerable improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a precise formula, by ascertaining if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two identical symmetrical numbers, A and B. Upon determining representability, we pinpoint an upper limit on the value of the smallest numerical component. We then prove that a certain set of numbers has a higher frequency of occurrence within the set of all natural numbers, N. We achieve analogous results when examining quotients of numbers whose binary format is anti-symmetric, meaning the second half mirrors the reverse of the first. In addition, the researchers investigate divisibility between two numbers, one of which is a palindrome and the other an anti-palindrome. They prove that a certain set of numbers, composed of products between palindromes and anti-palindromes, has a higher frequency of occurrence within the set of all natural numbers, N. We demonstrate the feasibility of obtaining exact intervals in which multiples of a number, N, that result from dividing two identical symmetrical numbers, A, and B. We accomplish analogous results for numbers whose binary format is anti-symmetric, meaning the second half mirrors the reverse of the first. In fact, the researchers even obtained exact intervals in which multiples

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting considerations for polyenergetic X-rays may result in image distortions and low signal precision, which poses significant challenges for both data analysts and algorithm developers. To address these issues, this study presents a comprehensive variational reconstruction model that accurately takes into account the effects of polyenergetic X-rays, simultaneously filtering out high frequency noise, while also differentiating between materials with distinct energy absorption characteristics. The proposed approach takes the form of a non-convex inverse problem with split operators, which includes three distinct components: a Chambolle-Lions type regularization term for denoising, a weighted Total Variation term for removing speckle noise, and a weighted Total Variation Laplacian term for improving image smoothness. The model is mathematically analyzed under optimal assumptions and experimental conditions, and its effectiveness is validated through numerical reconstructions of synthetic and real-world data.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge for training.  Traditional approaches to HTR rely heavily on data augmentation techniques, such as character-level augmentation, to increase training data visibility, but these methods fall short for characters with distinct shapes.  To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel data creation approach centered around word-level composition in a one-shot setting.  By employing pre-trained Language Models, we generate real-life handwritten sentences for recognition training, thereby enhancing the quality and diversity of the training dataset.  Compared to character-level augmentation, our method demonstrates improved accuracy on the IIIT Visual Genome and CAMILLE datasets under partial labelling.

We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly decreases the required memory by approximately two orders of magnitude, allowing us to compute three-nucleon interaction matrix elements with more precise limits in ab initio calculations. Our scheme enables us to reach higher energies of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements than was previously achievable. We have demonstrated that our storage approach leads to converged calculations for the ground-state energy of a certain nucleus. Our study further examined how the computational methods converge when calculating three-nucleon interactions. Our findings indicate that certain computationally costly elements can be disregarded due to being artifacts that vanish with more precise calculations. Our study ultimately shows that the ground-state energy of a certain nucleus agrees with its measured value. Our work now makes it possible to compute accurately heavy atomic nuclei through ab initio calculations.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the translation of amplitudes from the AdS$_5$ space to the conformal field theory plane, where the preamplitude can be computed via standard loop calculations. The approach, similar to twistor-holf constructs, relies on the dual representation of amplitudes to simplify the computation, yet differs in its application to a different type of dual representation. The development of an inverse M\"obius transformation plays a crucial role in the method. Although the formula is versatile, we demonstrate its application in the context of four graviton amplitudes. The formula incorporates the effects of two-loop dilaton and axion corrections, showcasing the balance between the dilaton and spinor-like modes.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a unique memory allocator that prioritizes memory access efficiency and a set of generic template tools to streamline CUDA programming.  By re-architecting the CUDA memory layout to resemble a contiguous array of object structures, DynaSOAr's allocator speeds up memory access and frees developers from tedious detail.  As evidence of its effectiveness, we successfully applied DynaSOAr to several practical applications, resulting in significant performance gains over existing CPU-based solutions.  Notably, DynaSOAr's allocator achieved speedups of up to 38x and 3x, respectively, for two prominent test cases.

We introduce family universal U(1)X models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, by defining U(1)X as a composite of SO(10) U(1)Y and U(1)χ gauge symmetries. To incorporate quantum gravity effects, we propose the introduction of a Dirac fermion χ as a dark matter candidate that's odd under gauged Z2 symmetry post U(1)X breaking, leading to a natural realization of isospin-violating dark matter with a natural f_n/f_p ratio of -0.7, thereby evading LUX, PANDAX and XENON1T experimental constraints. Furthermore, our work encompasses the investigation of masses and mixings for Higgs and gauge bosons, LHC constraints on Z' mass, dark matter direct and indirect detection experiments, resulting in viable parameter spaces for further study. To determine LHC Z' mass bounds for generic U(1)X models, four different scenarios are examined, with scenario II featuring family universal models possessing a natural f_n/f_p ratio of -0.7. To determine LHC Z' mass bounds for generic U(1)X models, four different scenarios are examined, with scenario II featuring family universal models possessing a natural f_n/f_p ratio of -0.7.

A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying equations that govern straw behavior when subjected to internal pressure are documented, alongside the introduction of an experimental approach in this paper to investigate strained, pressurized straw tubes. The presented research also focuses on measuring the Poisson's ratio of the straw wall for the NA62 spectrometer, with the ultimate goal of determining the optimal design limits to ensure the stable functioning of the detector.

In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority.
