They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
including higher-order effects of gravitational wave radiation, reveal that late-time
eccentricities of inspiraling binaries are typically underestimated by standard
models by up to 30 percent for heavy systems like 300-solar-mass binaries at
10 Hz, and less so for lighter binaries. By incorporating more refined equations,
a novel, accurate analytic formula for eccentricities at late times is formulated.
Furthermore, this model's results remain largely insensitive to the masses of the
binary components, with deviations below two percent, and generalizes previous
work by Peters and Mathews.

A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and the undulator taper technique to create a groundbreaking X-ray laser. This is made possible by using an XFELO to seed a free-electron laser (FEL) amplifier with a specially tailored electron beam. The unique characteristics of the beam allow for the tail to be within the gain bandwidth of XFELO, generating a lasing seed that's used for further amplification, while the leading part of the beam, outside XFELO's gain bandwidth, can still be utilized in the FEL amplifier. The suitability of naturally occurring "double-horn" beam current and residual energy chirp from a chicane compressor has also been identified. The outcome is potentially record-breaking levels of nearly terawatt X-ray pulses with superior shot-to-shot stability, paving the way for groundbreaking research across various fields.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes.  To address these limitations, we propose a new approach, called DyGED, for recognizing events in evolving networks using a combination of temporal self-attention and structural awareness.  Through extensive testing with diverse datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternative methods in accuracy, achieving up to an 8.5% improvement.  Notably, it also offers improved scalability compared to the best-performing models, along with insightful case studies that highlight its key features.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their comparison with numerical simulations, which includes an examination of how the self-similar exponent varies according to the law of the density variation and whether the energy source is sufficient to achieve singular solutions. Additionally, we investigate how an increase in the exponent according to a given power law leads to an initial nonlinear behavior in the self-similar solutions, which subsequently turns into a nonlinear convergence toward the corresponding self-similar solution as the impllosion progresses.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain when attempting to identify a randomly selected encoded text from multiple possible translations of an original message. Utilizing graph theory, the problem is approached by considering how connections between vertices in a graph relate to the adversary's guessing accuracy when the source is mapped to a subset of the graph's nodes. Additionally, we examine how a confidential message is protected when it is represented as a path in a graph, with the adversary's objective being to guess the specific path by sampling vertices along the graph's edges.

Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a prior in under-sampled synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image reconstruction, yet they're often impractical due to excessive generalization. This paper proposes MrSARP, a novel generative model that capitalizes on a hierarchical structure within the SAR data acquisition process. By incorporating prior knowledge about SAR geometry into a message-passing framework, MrSARP addresses the issue of over-sampling without resorting to synthetic data from a deep learning model. MrSARP exhibits superior performance in SAR image super-resolution and de-focusing applications, yielding reconstructing abilities on par with deep learning-trained models trained using high-resolution data.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework performs well even at slow circuit repetition rates and with minimal quantum circuit measurements, yielding a reliable energy estimate.  Moreover, we investigate how our approach handles noise during circuit operation, discovering that for short circuits it remains resistant to disturbances.  The outcome of these findings supports the use of the suggested method as an adaptable tool to exploit the mixed capabilities of QAOA within imperfect quantum devices.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The method has been developed into a reliable algorithm capable of accurately calculating the overlap area between two ellipses, provided that certain predefined conditions are met. The algorithm has been thoroughly tested and demonstrated to be both efficient and reliable, even when dealing with highly distorted ellipses that can be nearly tangent to each other. Developed applications utilizing the algorithm have showcased its effectiveness in solving real-world problems.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation and introduce the term "small q-function". The q-function has connections to both the instantaneous advantage rate function and the Hamiltonian. We develop a continuous-time "Q-learning" framework based on the q-function, separate from time discretization, by characterizing its relationship to value functions and stochastic processes via martingale conditions. We apply this theory to create new methods for high-resolution pricing and risk management in continuous time.

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but making predictions for multi-dimensional models like Hubbard is complicated due to computational and theoretical constraints. We investigated magnetic excitations of the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with longer-range hopping. Beginning with the 120-degree and striped patterns of magnetism, we used the self-consistent random phase approximation to determine magnon frequencies. We discovered a correlation in the striped phase related to a long-standing theoretical issue from the analogous Heisenberg model, where quantum fluctuations stabilize this pattern. We were able to outline the entire phase diagram using this new understanding and our results surprisingly matched recent numerical research. We compared our results with data on real triangular lattice materials and explored the link to a theoretically proposed state known as the chiral spin liquid phase.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset consisting of 302 CT images characterized by significant spinal pathologies, the proposed method achieved the highest identification rate of 97.4% and surpassed the best comparable approach, which reported an identification rate of 94.7%, by significantly reducing the relative error rate by 12.5%.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. This study applies the mathematical structure of Markovian jump processes to the theoretical analysis of flux cumulants. The asymptotic characteristics of flux cumulants are independent of how the current is defined, due to a mathematical property known as gauge invariance. This theoretical result is applicable to a broad range of systems, including Markovian models of lactose permease and a model of a molecular motor called F1F1. The data from an experimental study of an artificial motor system, called the cytoplasmic coupling factor F1F0, is also examined in terms of these asymptotic characteristics.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified mathematical characteristics, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it shows that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it investigates the impact of mathematical transformations known as symplectic birational transformations on relative quantum cohomology. For a given mathematical relationship involving the transversality condition, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions can be connected directly under these transformations. This research has implications for the study of quantum cohomology in the context of mathematical transformations.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for materials of any shape and orientation, and is demonstrated through experiments involving particular cuts of zinc oxide crystals.

We explore a cutting-edge method for optically driving and controlling the flow of non-linear polariton waves within a micro-cavity setup, enabling the creation of complex optical patterns. The polariton waves, resulting from the interaction between photons and quantum dots, exhibit unique properties akin to those of plasmons. By harnessing this system, researchers can manipulate the direction of polariton flow and create discrete, nanoscale channels that control the propagation of polariton pulses. The system's responsiveness to external stimuli allows for the rapid reconfiguration of these optical channels, and the coexistence of multiple polariton modes facilitates the generation of intricate, quasi-periodic optical structures. The discussed approach holds promise for developing sophisticated all-optical micro-devices, encompassing analog photonic computing systems and optical memory components.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22 b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope, with wavelengths of 0.48 and 2.1 microns, are presented during a period of reduced dust activity, revealing a refined upper limit of the planet's radius of approximately 4500 km. Medium-depth transit observations also suggest particle sizes ranging from 0.5 to 1 micron, suggesting extremely high mass loss rates of about 3e8 kg/s, consistent with predictions from theoretical models based on carbon-rich compositions. Variations in grain size and albedo are examined, including scenarios of accretion of small particles onto larger particles, which could mitigate mass loss rates - however, these changes cannot fully explain the observed differences between paired spectra. Our findings indicate the likelihood of a short-lived (typically less than 1 year), intense mass loss phase, possibly triggered by a massive celestial event, such as a comet or asteroid collision, that has not been detected through current observational methods.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates machine learning algorithms and statistical tools, in addition to linear algebra operations (matrix multiplication, linear systems resolution, SVD, eigenvalue decomposition) and data plotting functionality.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting he lacked a significant mathematical contribution relevant to his famous controversy with the Catholic Church.  It is proposed here that his actual contribution was to defend science from philosophical objections leveled by the Church, requiring no advanced mathematics to accomplish.  Furthermore, it is suggested that Bellarmine's compromise, offering a possible solution to the problem of motion based on an equilibrium of forces, was already being considered by Galileo, indicating Bellarmine's understanding of scientific principles did not preclude him from being a churchman.  Ultimately, it is proposed here that Galileo's reputation as the hero of the scientific revolution has been overstated, with his true significance having been exaggerated over time.

The increasing popularity of Tsallis' thermodynamic framework is largely attributed to its capability to describe phenomena exhibiting anomalous thermal properties, which requires adherence to generalized thermal equilibrium. Our study focuses on examining non-Gaussian influences on Saha's ionization through the application of Tsallis statistics. We addressed this challenge by generalizing the number density with a non-Gaussian distribution based on Fermi-Dirac theory and then formulated the Saha equation for cosmological recombination. Our analysis reveals two novel non-Gaussian impacts:  the establishment of two distinct equilibrium conditions and the identification of a hydrogen binding energy related to q-value. Our results show that a minute 'a-parameter' is required to generate continuous distributions of ionized and bound particles, thereby supporting the notion of non-Gaussian effects during the recombination period. Furthermore, our findings indicate that non-Gaussian thermal fluctuations could potentially influence particle distribution during the recombination period. We hope that our findings will spark the development of novel non-Gaussian thermal fluctuation theories.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed embedded PIC regions, and full PIC simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates good agreement among the models, with notably large adaptable PIC regions required within the MHD domain to achieve such convergence.

This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced professional in the field of computer science.  Over time, this assistant becomes an essential and indispensable tool, capable of providing independent support and performing a variety of autonomous tasks.
